HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer -

HELD: Sulphuric acid (Spent) - Rule 57G declaration filed is adequate for acid also as the input too suffered duty as sulphuric acid. "As long as the material, spent sulphuric acid, had paid duty under Heading 2807.00 as sulphuric acid, the Rule 57G declaration by the recipient manufacturer of sulphuric acid as input cannot be held to be not applicable for spent sulphuric acid. The inputs had suffered duty as sulphuric acid and the declaration of inputs as sulphuric acid was adequate in the circumstances. In the circumstances, Stay sought by the department is not warranted. The application is accordingly rejected."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - inputs--detailed description in prescribed manner is necessary to avail of credit

HELD: MODVAT--Detailed description in the prescribed manner of inputs is necessary to avail of MODVAT credit. "......the proforma for declaration to be filed under Rule 57G also has specific columns for the description of the final product and its Tariff classification as well as description of the inputs and its Tariff classification, besides the column to indicate the nature of the inputs whether raw material or component etc. When such is the legal position, and such is the requirement of the proforma for the declaration prescribed for the purpose, the contention of the appellants that broad description of the inputs will suffice for the purpose of availing MODVAT credit, is not tenable.'

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Declaration--Inputs must be specifically declared for availing of credit

FACT: The issue to be determined in this Revenue appeal is whether, in order to avail Modvat credit, it is mandatory to specifically mention the inputs in the declaration filed under Rule 57G of Central Excise Rules, 1944 or it is sufficient to mention the Tariff heading under which these items are classified.

HELD: Modvat credit--availment of Modvat credit cannot be permitted when the inputs have not been specifically mentioned in the declaration filed under Rule 57G [ratio of earlier decision in Paro Food Products v. CCE 1988 (19) ECR 127]. "........in interpreting the scope and ambit of Rule 57G(2) the Tribunal has in a number of decisions taken the view that the manufacturer who fails to file a declaration under Rule 57G specifying the particular input would not be entitled to take credit of duty paid on the inputs received by him under the MODVAT Scheme. .......in view of the decisions quoted above........the appeal is allowed."

., 11-5-1987 to 15-4-2000. Under this amended rule 57E, the right of the manufacturer to obtain additional modvat credit in respect of inputs, on which further duty had been paid for any reason subsequent to the date of the receipt of inputs by the manufacturer, is recognized. However, such right accrues to the manufacturer subject to his complying with the procedure of adjustment contemplated in rule 57E, as amended. [Para 2] The above discussion indicates that the right to claim modvat credit existed only in rule 57A. Even rule 57E says so. There can be no doubt that right from its inception, the right to claim modvat credit is under rule 57A. Rule 57A recognizes the right of the manufacturer to claim credit. Rule 57E recognizes not only the right of the manufacturer to claim credit but also the extent to which credit could be claimed for the duty paid on inputs. Therefore, rule 57A is a substantive provision. However, the procedure of adjustment finds place in rule 57E. Rule 57E is procedural provision. It deals with adjustments in duty credit. The object behind enacting rules 57A, 57E and 57G is to avoid duty on duty, whereby the price of the final product is loaded. Therefore, rule 57A recognizes the right of the manufacturer to take credit for the specified duty paid on the inputs, whereas rule 57E deals with adjustments in the duty credit. Such adjustments mean [adjustments] on account of reduction on the credit allowed. It could also be in the event of refund. Suffice it to state that the rule 57E deals only with adjustment in the duty credit. Rule 57G states that credit shall not be taken unless the manufacturer of the final product maintains his records regarding receipt of the inputs in his factory like bill of entry, certain types of registers (RR-1) or any other document prescribed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs. [Para 3]

Therefore, the Courts below were right in holding that rule 57E was procedural, clarificatory and, therefore, would not affect the substantive right of the manufacturer of the specified final product to claim modvat credit for the duty paid on the inputs subsequent to the date of the receipt of those inputs. Consequently, the assessee-manufacturer was entitled to take credit [of duty in respect of inputs utilized] between the period 16-8-1987 to 30-12-1987. [Para 4]

Accordingly, the appeal was to be dismissed.

V. Shekhar, Ajay Sharma, Pradeep K. Dubey, Sudhir Kr. Sajwan and B. Krishna Prasad for the Appellant. Amit Kumar Sharma, Gaurav Goel, Mahesh Agrawala, E.C. Agrawal and Rishi Agrawala for the Respondent.

made applicable. That could be called as a procedural lapse. In this case, a photocopy of the invoice cannot be recognised either as an original or duplicate or triplicate or quadruplicate. It is no document at all in terms of the Rules. Therefore, the requirement of rule 52A(4) of the Rules having not been complied with, the assessee has been rightly denied the benefit of credit as applicable under rule 57G of the Rules. [Para 4.5] Therefore, the Tribunal was correct in denying the Modvat Credit in respect of clearance made in violation of rule 52A(4) based on photocopies of documents, which is no document at all as per the Rules. [Para 4.7]

II. Credit available when original copy available

As regards another credit, there was an original copy of the invoice available along with the duty paid inputs, even though the duplicate copy was not available. Therefore, the issue raised gets covered by rule 57G(11) of the rules and the decision of the Allahabad High Court in CCE v. Hindalco Industries Ltd.2013 (293) ELT 208 is squarely applicable to this issue. Therefore, credit was held allowable. [Paras 5.1 and 5.2]

III. Penalty

In the present case the goods have been supplied by Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, a Government of India Undertaking, and the department has accepted the plea that the entire inputs have suffered duty. However, the only reason attributable for levy of penalty is that the goods were not accompanied with proper invoices, as required under rule 52A(4) of the Rules. From a reading of the orders of the Tribunal and the authorities below, it is clear that the appellant had no intention either to evade payment of duty or to avail duty wrongfully. In such view of the matter, the penalty imposed on the assessee was set aside in both the cases. [Para 6.3]

FACT: The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. HELD: The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Thus, in view of the subsequent amendment made in rule 57G by Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT) dated 9-2-1999, the MODVAT credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in the duty-paying documents. The Board had also clarified, vide Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX dated 23-2-1999, that Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT), has been issued so as to empower the Assistant Commissioner, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer, to allow the credit ignoring minor procedural lapses provided the inputs have suffered duty and are being used in the process of manufacture. FACT: Facts [Hindustan Zinc]

In case of Hindustan Zinc Ltd., assessee obtained zinc ore concentrate [Zinc Sulphide (ZnS)] from the mines on payment of excise duty which is used as an input for the production of zinc.

When ZnS is heated (calcined) at high temperature in the presence of oxygen, zinc oxide (ZnO) and sulphuric acid are produced.

Zinc Oxide is further oxidised to produce zinc.

Sulphur obtained as a technological necessity is a pollutant and is, therefore, converted into sulphur dioxide in the presence of catalysts like Vanadium Pentaoxide & Hydrogen Peroxide. Sulphuric acid is converted into sulphur and the assessee did not take any Cenvat Credit on the inputs used after the emergence of sulphur dioxide.

The sulphuric acid produced as a by-product is sold on payment of excise duty to various industries.

In some cases, sulphuric acid was sold under exemption for use in/as fertilizers.

The Department argued that as per rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 (Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004), the assessee was obliged to maintain separate accounts and records for the inputs used in the production of zinc and sulphuric acid and in the absence of the same the assessee was obliged to pay 8% as an amount on the sale price of exempt sulphuric acid.

The assessee argued that the very purpose of the grant of exemption to sulphuric acid was to keep the input costs at the lowest for the production of fertilizers during the relevant period. Fertilizers themselves were wholly exempted from the payment of excise duty because the government wanted the farmgate price to the farmer should be at the lowest. In fact, the government grants subsidies to the fertilizer plants for the difference between the cost of production and sale price determined by the government. Any duty demand on the sulphuric acid will defeat the very purpose of grant of exemption and make the fertilizer cost higher than the desirable level. In such a scenario, such higher cost will have to be compensated by the government as subsidy.

As an alternative, it was pleaded that even if rule 57 CC is to be held as intra vires, the demand raised in the show cause notices will not survive on proper interpretation of rule 57CC of the Rules and hence is to be quashed.

These arguments may seem to be attractive. However, having regard to the processes involved, which is already explained above and the reasons afforded earlier, these submissions were not persuasive. [Para 25]

Furthermore, the provisions of rule 57CC cannot be read in isolation. In order to understand the scheme of Modvat Credit contained in this Rule, a combined reading of rule 57A, 57B and 57D along with rule 57CC becomes inevitable. It can be easily discerned from a combined reading of the aforesaid provisions that the terms used are 'inputs', 'final products', 'by-product', 'waste products' etc. These terms have been used taking into account commercial reality in trade. In that context when we scan through rule 57CC, reference to final product being manufactured with the same common inputs becomes understandable. This Rule did not talk about emergence of final product and a by-product and still said that rule 57CC will apply. The department seeks to apply rule 57CC when rule 57D does not talk about application of rule 57CC to final product and by-product when the by-product emerged as a technological necessity. Accepting the argument of the Revenue would amount to equating by-product and final product thereby obliterating the difference though recognised by the legislation itself. [Para 26]

So long as a product is obtained as a by-product and not as a final product, rule 57CC will not apply. [Para 27]

IV. Filing of writ petition valid, as Rule itself was challenged :

Revenue argued about non-maintainability of the writ petition filed by Hindustan Zinc Limited before the High Court. No doubt, it had filed writ petition at show cause stage. That was a reason because of which the writ petitions were entertained, and rightly so, it is a different matter that while interpreting the rule, the High Court chose to read down the said rule and to give an interpretation which would save it from the vice of unconstitutionality.

Moreover, other statutory appeal filed by the Department is against the order of CESTAT, which involves same question. Matter is argued in appeal also at length and Supreme Court was deciding the same on merits. For all these reasons the argument of alternate remedy has to be discarded. [Para 28]

Facts [Birla Copper]

In another cases pertaining to Birla Copper, the manufacturing process of copper from the copper ore concentrate was similar to that of zinc and the emergence of sulphuric acid as a by-product was conceded. Department raised similar demand in respect of exempt sales of sulphuric acid.

Facts [Rallis India]

In case of Rallis India Ltd., assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Gelatin for use in pharmaceutical industry for manufacture of capsules.

Gelatin was produced by reacting Hydrochloric Acid with bovine animal bones.

During the reaction, the bone converts into ossein which in turn is used to produce gelatin. The inorganic substances like phosphorous etc. are washed with water which is called mother liquor, spent liquor or phosphoral liquor.

When these by- products and waste products are cleared without payment of duty, the Excise Department demanded duty @ 8% in terms of rule 57CC.

Issue Involved

Whether Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 [Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004] is applicable to sale of exempt by-products ?

HELD: I. Sulphuric Acid is a by-product and its emerges by itself mandatorily

Sulphuric acid is indeed a by-product. In fact, it is so treated by the assessee in their balance sheet as well as various other documents which were filed by the assessee in the courts below. It is also a common case of the parties that assessee viz. Hindustan Zinc Limited and Birla Copper were established to produce zinc and copper respectively and not for the production of sulphuric acid. It was undisputed that emergence of sulphur dioxide in the calcination process of concentrated ore is a technological necessity and then conversion of the same into sulphuric acid as a non-polluting measure cannot elevate the sulphuric acid to the status of final product. Technologically, commercially and in common parlance, sulphuric acid is treated as a by-product in extraction of non-ferrous metals by companies not only in India but all over the world. [Para 16]

II. No part of input was used for production of 'sulphuric acid' :

Ore concentrates (Zinc or Copper) are completely utilised for the production of zinc and copper and no part of the metal, zinc or copper forms part of the sulphuric acid which is cleared out. The extraction of zinc from the ore concentrate will inevitably result in the emergence of sulphur dioxide as a technological necessity. Assessee cannot use lesser quantity of zinc concentrate only to produce the metal and not produce sulphur dioxide. In other words, a given quantity of zinc concentrate will result in emergence of zinc sulphide and sulphur dioxide according to the chemical formula on which assessee have no control. [Para 17]

Hence, ore concentrate is completely consumed in the extraction of zinc and no part of the metal is forming part of sulphuric acid. [Para 18]

The assessee have consumed the entire quantity of zinc concentrate in the production of zinc. [Para 19]

III. Percentage payment under Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 (Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004) is inapplicable in respect of by-products viz. 'sulphuric acid' :

Rule 57CC requires an assessee to maintain separate records for inputs which are used in the manufacture of two or more final products one of which is dutiable and the other is non-dutiable. In that event, rule 57 CC will apply. For example, a tyre manufacturer manufactures different kinds of tyres, one or more of which were exempt like tyre used in animal carts and cycle tyre, where car tyres and truck tyres attract excise duty. The rubber, the accelerators, the retarders, the fillers, sulphur, vulcanising agents which are used in production of tyres are indeed common to both dutiable and exempt tyres. Such assessees are mandated to maintain separate records to avoid the duty demand of 8% on exempted tyres. [Para 20]

The applicant has requested for rectification of the error in the Tribunal's order because its declaration was filed on 31.3.1986 and duly acknowledged by the Superintendent.

HELD: Modvat--the applicant is eligible for Modvat for 1.4.1986 because its declaration under Rule 57G was filed with the Range Supdt. on 31.3.1986. "The Tribunal has given a finding in the impugned order that the petitioner would not be entitled to the Modvat benefit for the inputs in question for the period prior to 2.4.1986 on the ground that the declaration under Rule 57-G has been acknowledged by the jurisdictional Collector only on 2.4.1986 and under Rule 57G(2) a manufacturer who has filed a declaration under sub-rule (1) may after obtaining the acknowledgement of the Asst. Collector take the credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. On going through the records we find that on 31.3.1986 the petitioner has addressed a communication to the Asst. Collector purporting to be a declaration under Rule 57-G of the Modvat Rules. This was presented with the Range Supdt., Hyderabad and has been acknowledged by him on 31.3.1986. It has been forwarded to the Asst. Collector, Hyderabad who had received it on 2.4.1986. It is not disputed that the inputs in question have suffered duty and the petitioner would be otherwise eligible to Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question. Filing of a declaration under Rule 57-G is a procedural formality and in the present case the same has been done on 31.3.1986 itself to the Range Supdt. The fact that the Range Supdt. forwarded the same to the Assistant Collector in the same place only on 2.4.1986 cannot be a reason to deny the petitioner the benefit of Modvat credit. The Board has also given a clarification in this regard.........the impugned order is amended by rectifying the error holding that the petitioner would be entitled to the Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question taken on 1.4.1986. The impugned order would stand modified accordingly after rectification of this mistake."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Assessee was availing MODVAT credit on basis of invoices issued by dealers/traders - MODVAT credit was denied to assessee on ground that duty paying documents did not show required details - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed said order - As per relevant Board Circular, Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in manufacturing process - Whether Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of appeal, should have considered Board’s Circular - Held, yes - Whether since assessee demonstrated that it had received duty paid inputs and consumed same in its factory, assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit - Held, yes [Para 5] Circular and notification : Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty.

On appeal :

HELD: It was undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. From the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. The Board, in the above Circular had clearly mentioned for disposal of pending cases accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of the appeal, should have considered the Board’s Circular while dismissing the appeal filed by the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee demonstrated that it had received the duty paid inputs and consumed the same in its factory and, hence, it was eligible for MODVAT credit. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, read with section 2(h) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Assessee was a job worker for company EUAL - It manufactured wet grinders out of raw material supplied by EUAL under cover of invoice under rule 57G - Whether in view of Rado Tyres Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise 2004 (174) ELT 218 (Bang. - Trib.) transfer of input to job worker amounted to sale within meaning of section 2(h) and Modvat credit was available to assessee on inputs supplied by EUAL under cover - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-job worker manufactured wet grinder for company EUAL out of the raw material supplied by EUAL under cover of invoice issued under rule 57G. On the basis of the said invoice issued, the assessee availed Modvat credit. However, the department took the view that no ‘sale’ was involved in supply of goods to assessee by EUAL and, therefore, the invoices were not valid documents for the purpose of availment of Modvat on those goods. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the entitlement of Modvat credit to the assessee.

On appeal:

HELD: In the decision Rado Tyres Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise 2004 (174) ELT 218 (Bang. - Trib.), the Tribunal held that transfer of input to the job worker amounted to ‘sale’ within the meaning of section 2(h) and, therefore, the invoices showing payment of duty and other particulars were valid documents for availment of input duty credit by the job worker.

Therefore, it would be held that the assessee had rightly availed Modvat credit on the inputs supplied by EUAL under cover of rule 57G. In the result, the impugned order stood upheld. [Para 3]

The appeal of the revenue was dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Inputs--Oxygen and Acetylene used in cutting torch are inputs for Modvat credit to the extent used for manufacture of the specified finished product

FACT: The Collector (Appeals) rejected the appellants' claim for Modvat credit in respect of oxygen and acetylene on the ground that these gases were used in the cutting torch which comes under the excluded category in Rule 57A.

HELD: Modvat--Inputs--Oxygen and acetylene gases--The appellants can avail of the benefit of Modvat credit under Rule 57A in respect of oxygen and acetylene but only for the quantity used for manufacture of the specified finished product (ratio of Tribunal decisions). ".......we find no reason to depart from the above decisions and therefore hold that the appellants' plea is maintainable in law. We however, observe that MODVAT Credit can be given only in respect of that quantity of oxygen & Acetylene used in or in relation to the manufacture of specified finished product and not for other uses in the appellant's factory. The appeal is thus allowed in the above terms."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - Silicone spray is an input for plastic moulded components. It increases the output of moulds and improves their quality. It is not a tool. Modvat admissible

FACT: During the process of injection moulding of thermoplastic components 'Silicone Spray' is applied to the mould surface as it provides lubrication and facilitates easy detachment of the moulded components from the moulds, thus contributing to better productivity. The issue for determination is whether 'Silicone Spray' can be considered as an 'input' used in the manufacture of the final product, thus being eligible for Modvat credit, or whether it is excluded from the scope of the term 'input' in terms of the Explanation to Rule 57A.

HELD: Modvat--'Silicone Spray' is to be considered as an input used in the manufacture of plastic moulded components. It is a chemical that increases the output of the moulding machine and improves the quality of the final product and cannot be deemed as a tool or appliance that is excluded from the purview of Modvat credit. "Having regard to the scientific and technical meaning of the term 'appliance' which was referred to in the Tribunal's decision in the case of Collector of Central Excise v. Weldeker Laminates........and even on the basis of the common understanding of the term 'appliance', I am of the view that 'Silicon Spray' which is in the nature of a chemical cannot be deemed as an 'appliance' or 'equipment' which are excluded from the purview of the MODVAT scheme in terms of the 'Explanation' to the notification No. 217/86. In a number of decisions of the Tribunal it has been held that for availing MODVAT it is not necessary that the input should form a part of the final product. For these reasons and also for the reason that use of 'Silicon Spray' on the moulds during the injection moulding adds to the output of the machine and improves the quality of the moulded product, it has to be held that it is an input used in the manufacture of the final product. ........In view of the above discussion and on the ratio of the Tribunal's decision quoted above the impugned orders are set aside and appeals are allowed with consequential relief to the appellants."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Applicability - Assessee claimed Modvat Credit on Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) used as fuel for generating electricity captively consumed for manufacture of final products such as caustic soda and cement - Whether since without utilization of LSHS it was not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda, LSHS would come within ambit of expression ‘used in relation to manufacture of final product’ in rule 57A and, therefore, assessee was entitled to Modvat credit on LSHS under Explanation (c) to rule 57A - Held, yes (Para 8) Words and Phrases : Expression, ‘used in or in relation to manufacture of final product’ as appearing in rule 57A of Central Excise Rules, 1944 Circulars and Notification : Notification No. 4/94 dated 1-3-1994

FACT: The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Iron or Steel--waste--(re-rollable)--deemed credit has to be given for 1.4.1987 to 30.8.1987 @ Rs. 365/-in view of commitment in Trade Notice

HELD: Modvat--Deemed credit on re-rollable waste and scrap of Iron or Steel for the period from 1.4.1987 to 30.8.1987 upheld in view of statutory direction to this effect, "We have gone through the statutory direction issued under Rule 57G(2) of the Central Excise Rules......The Chandigarh Collectorate has also published a Trade Notice No. 43/87 dated 30.10.1987 to the effect that with effect from 1.4.1987 ingots and re-rollable materials of iron or steel purchased from outside may be deemed to have paid duty at Rs. 365 per tonne and credit of duty in respect of such ingots and re-rollable materials used is allowed without production of documents evidencing the payment of duty. We would, therefore hold that by virtue of a statutory direction the appellant should be held to have properly availed the deemed Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - Spent sulphuric acid--Classification--Having been sold for fertilizers it falls U/CETA: 38.23; eligible for Modvat as it is not sulphuric acid but a mfrd. product. CE

HELD: The Asstt. Collector approved the appellants' classification of spent sulphuric acid, produced as a by-product, U/CH 28 but reversed Modvat as it was neither a manufactured product nor waste exempted U/Notfn. 81/75-CE when used in fertilizers. The Collector (Appeals) held the item fell U/CET H. 38.23. The Tribunal upholding the classification U/H 38.23 held that spent acid was not sulphuric acid but was a manufactured product as it was sold for use in fertilisers. Modvat was, therefore, not to be denied.

HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963 -Interpretation of entries in the schedule - whether "industrial stearine fatty acid" would fall under the category "acid"? - Held yes - Kerala general sales tax act, 1963 - First schedule entry 65

HELD: Held that - so long as the Industrial Stearine Fatty Acid is commercially and chemically known as acid, that will surely fall within the ambit of the Entry 65 of the First Schedule to the Act. (Para 5)

scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9] For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - additional duty subsequently collected from the input manufacturer is also allowable to the manufacturer of final product

HELD: Since indisputably the input has suffered additional duty for the like sum, the appellants are entitled to Modvat credit for the amount in question. "...in the facts and circumstances of the case, the appellants would be entitled to take Modvat credit for the amount in question, since indisputably the input has suffered additional duty for the like sum. We would like to make it clear that under the Modvat Scheme there is no specific provision for granting refund of the amount to the appellant in cash."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Refractories are not inputs for Modvat in Steel Industry

FACT: Iron & Steel products are manufactured by the appellants. They filed a declaration under Rule 57G of CE Rules for availing MODVAT benefit in respect of inputs used in relation to their manufacture of finished products. The Assistant Collector held that the refractory products are not covered by the explanation in Rule 57A of CE Rules. This order was upheld by Collector (Appeal).

HELD: Modvat: Inputs--Refractories used in the steel industry are not inputs as per Explanation under Rule 57A, and hence are not eligible for Modvat. ".. ...we hold that refractories used in the steel industry are hit by the explanation to Rule 57A, because of the fact that they go in relation to the machinery and form part of the machinery and equipment and therefore the authorities below are justified in disallowing the credit in respect of the duty paid on this item."

Ltd.--Rule 57-5 would not be attracted-Section 11-A is not attracted as ground plan was approved by the Department and a separate registration certified was obtained-The demand of central excise duty and penalty set aside-Appeal allowed (Paras 22, 23) HELD: We also find that since a separate registration certificate was obtained by which the ground plan was approved by the Central Excise Department, there was no case made out for attracting Section 11A of the Act as there was no intention to evade the payment of duty nor HBSA Pvt. HEADNOTE: Section 35G of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Appeal to High Court - Modvat - Recovery again after reversing irregular - No question of confirming order - CE Rule 571 - Stay - Waiver of recovery allowed - Plant  machinery nor process of manufacture to be interfered with

FACT: Though the applicants have reversed the Modvat credit alleged to have been taken irregularly, the demand for duty payable on the final product has been confirmed for an equal amount. The plant and machinery has been confiscated with an option to redeem on payment of fine of Rs. 25,000/-. This application is for stay and waiver of pre-deposit of duty amounting to Rs. 5,22,823/-.

HELD: When the Modvat credit alleged to have been taken irregularly has been reversed, the question of demanding duty again to the same extent and of confirming the demand does not arise. Stay of recovery of duty granted. The Deptt. should lift the detention made for recovery of duty. Plant and machinery should not be disposed of and normal process of manufacture not to be interfered with. "Hence when the MODVAT Credit alleged to have been taken irregularly has been reversed, the question of demanding duty again to the same extent alleging short levy and confirming the demand does not arise. Only where there is no balance in the MODVAT account, there is a requirement of making good the short levy by deposit in the PLA. In this prima facie view of the matter, we grant and stay and waiver of recovery of the duty amount and also direct the Departmental authorities to lift the detention alleged to have been made for recovery of the duty amount. ...........The plant and machinery ordered confiscation should not be disposed of by the Department and the normal process of manufacture should not be interfered with till the disposal of the appeal."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 2004 - Modvat Credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Period November and December, 1995 - Whether amendment made in rule 57G by insertion of sub-rule (11) vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 relates to procedure for availing Modvat credit and does not affect any substantive right - Held, yes - Whether Modvat credit would not be denied only on ground that documents referred to in sub-rule (2) of rule 57G does not strictly comply with said rule where said documents contain details of payment dues, description of goods, assessable value, name and address of factory or warehouse etc. - Held, yes - Assessee, a manufacturer had availed Modvat credit on duty paid inputs - Asstt. Commissioner disallowed said credit on ground that invoice in question was not marked as duplicate as according to him during relevant period, in view of rule 57G Modvat credit could be allowed only on furnishing of duplicate invoice and not otherwise - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order - However Tribunal held that after amendment of rule 57G vide Notification No. 7/99-CE(NT), dated 9-2-1999 credit cannot be denied on minor procedural lapses in case inputs are duty paid, and in view of Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 said amendment will applicable to all pending cases - Tribunal accordingly held that assessee was entitled for benefit of Modvat credit - Whether no infirmity could be found in impugned order of Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 35, 36, and 39] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture and sale of aluminium products. The Assistant Commissioner, denied Modvat credit on inputs on the grounds that the words 'duplicate invoice' was not mentioned and in one invoice, the portion showing the words 'original and duplicate' was torn and according to Rule 57G as it stood during the relevant period, Modvat credit could have been allowed only on furnishing of duplicate invoice and not otherwise. The Commissioner (Appeals) had also upheld the disallowance of Modvat credit. However, the Tribunal had held that after the amendment of Rule 57G vide Notification No. 7/99-CE(NT), dated 9th February, 1999 the credit cannot be denied on minor procedural lapses in case the inputs were duty paid and further in view of Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 that amendment would apply to all pending cases. The Tribunal, accordingly, held that assessee was entitled for the benefit of Modat credit in respect of the impugned inputs.

On appeal:

HELD: It is not in dispute that the assessee while making purchases in question has paid the applicable central excise duty. The only defect/lacunae in the process of availing Modvat credit was that the invoice was not marked as 'duplicate'. Rest of the particulars mentioned in that invoice are not in dispute nor its correctness is being disputed by the revenue. [Para 8]

In the instant case the assessee is the person who issues the invoice. Procedure to be observed by the manufacturer who wants to avail Modvat credit is provided by Rule 57G. The manufacturer who intends to take credit of the duty paid on inputs should file a declaration with the Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over his factory indicating the inputs intended to be used in the final product. Such a manufacture who has filed a declaration is allowed to take credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. Clause (2) states that no credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in his factory or any other document as may be prescribed by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette in this behalf evidencing payment of duty on such inputs. By Notification No. 23/94, dated 20-5-1994, it was provided that this duplicate copy is the one to be used for taking credit under rule 57G and rule 57T. [Para 9]

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in various cases to the facts of the instant case, it was to be held that the amendment made in rule 57G of the Rules by insertion of sub-rule (11) vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 relates to procedure for availing Modvat credit and does not effect any substantive right. [Para 35]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Main question involved is whether a fresh declaration to required to be submitted under Rule 57-G for claiming benefit of modvat, credit after exceeding the small scale industries (SSI) limit - The respondent had submitted declaration under Rule 57-G to claim modvat credit on the inputs - However as the respondent was within the SSI exemption limit under Notification No. 175/86 no claim of any credit was made - When SSI limit exceeded the respondent started claiming Modvat credit - No fresh declaration was filed - Held - under Rule 57-G of the Rules, declaration regarding inputs as well as the final product is required to be indicated - A declaration filed once is good unless there is change in the aforesaid items - No fresh declaration is required

HELD: Under Rule 57G of the Rules, declaration regarding inputs as well as the final product is required to be indicated. A declaration filed once is good unless there is change in the aforesaid items. In the present case, there was neither any change in the inputs nor in the final product. (Para 9)

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Modvat - Nitrogen gas for inert atmosphere for mfre. of MMA Monomer eligible

FACT: The appellants claimed Modvat benefit for Nitrogen Gas as an input used in relation to their final product MMA Monomer. The gas was used as it was inert, did not react with other chemicals, and was an essential technological necessity to create an inert atmosphere. The Assistant Collector held that such a use of Nitrogen gas cannot be held to be in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and therefore disallowed the credit. The Collector (Appeals) concurred with this view.

HELD: Creation of inert atmosphere is for manufacture of MMA Monomer as without such an inert atmosphere final product could not be manufactured. "........creation of such an atmosphere is only for the purpose of manufacture of MMA Monomer, as, without such an inert atmosphere, the final product could not be manufactured."

2. The process of manufacture and use of Nitrogen gas indicates that the same has to be taken as used in relation to the manufacture of MMA Monomer.".......the process of manufacture and the stage and purpose of use of Nitrogen gas, clearly indicates that the same has to be taken as used "in relation to the manufacture" of MMA Monomer."

3. Nitrogen gas held as used in relation to manufacture of MMA Monomer and eligible for Modvat credit. ".......with the use of Nitrogen gas as indicated, the same has to be taken as used in relation to manufacture of MMA Monomer and eligible to availment of credit vide Rule 57A of the Rules. The demand raised and the order confirming the same, therefore, cannot be sustained and has to be set aside."

HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule 57Q of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Input tax credit -  Assessee was engaged in manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing unit known as 'H' - During set up of 'H', assessee purchased complete Single Point Mooring system [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc. - SPM system was located by assessee outside factory premises - Assessee availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it fell within definition of capital goods under rule 57Q - Lower Authorities disallowed Modvat credit - Whether SPM system though located outside factory fell within definition of capital goods under rule 57Q - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was entitled to Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system - Held, yes [Para 21][In favour of assessee]GST/Modvat credit: Where assessee during set up of its factory purchased complete Single Point Mooring System (SPM system) along with accessories and located it outside factory premises, SPM system fell within definition of capital goods and assessee was entitled to Modvat credit of duty paid on said system

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

It availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it was capital goods in terms of rule 57Q.

The lower authorities including the Tribunal disallowed the Modvat credit.

On appeal to High Court:

HELD: The Single Point Mooring (SPM) buoy is located in mid sea (Arabian Sea), off. Suvail Coast, in Magdalla Port territorial water, at a distance of approx 12 kms from tank farm. SPM is a floating platform, held in place by 6 sets of suitable mooring chains which in turn are either connected to a pile or an anchor. SPM holds a vessel through a mooring hawser. SPM has an arrangement of inbuilt pipeline system with its entry/exit points, where subsea and floating hoses connect to facilitate the transfer of cargo between the vessel and the terminal. The floating hoses are connected to the vessel's manifold. Vessel pump the cargo through these hoses. [Para 9]

The subsea hoses are connected to a hard pipe lines at the bottom of the sea. This hard pipe is in turn connected to the tank farms located within the factory premises of the assessee. Accordingly SPM is connected to the tank farm through 2 pipelines. One pipeline is used for transporting Naphtha and other petroleum products from SPM to the tank farm. The second line is used to transport Paraxylene from SPM to the tank farm. These pipelines run underwater on the sea bed for about 4.85 kms and are then buried underground for another 7.15 kms to reach the assessee's tank farm. SPM is used for unloading of imported and coastal consignments and pumping the raw materials, namely, Naptha, Paraxylene and other petroleum products through the pipe lines directly to the tanks within the factory. [Para 10]

Part of the pipelines and SPM are integrally connected with the equipments and tanks within the factory through the pipelines and instrumentation. It is necessary to run the refinery of the size in question without installation of SPM used in connection with the import of crude by giant crude tankers. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Modvat - Hydrochloric/Sulphuric Acid, Hydrazine and Sodium Sulphate used in paper manufacture for demineralisation of water or as dc-oxidants are entitled to Modvat benefit

FACT: In the process of manufacturing paper, hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid are used for demineralisation of water which is then turned into steam which is used for the drying of paper. Hydrazine 100% and Sodium Sulphate are used as deoxidants to carry oxygen in the water treatment plants. The issue that arises for determination is whether the items mentioned above can be considered as inputs used in relation to the manufacture of paper, thus being entitled to MODVAT Credit.

HELD: MODVAT--Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, hydrozine 100% and sodium sulphate used in the manufacture of paper are eligible for MODVAT credit as subject inputs have a nexus with a process which is integrally connected with the ultimate production of paper (ratio of earlier decision in Andhra Pradesh Paper Mills Ltd. v. CCE). ".......following the ratio of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and of this Tribunal........we hold that both Hydrochloric and Sulphuric Acid would be eligible for the benefit of MODVAT Credit, as these are used for treatment of water as seen from the order of the lower appellate authority. So far as Hydrazene 100% is concerned, it is also used for treatment of water. Its use is for the generation of steam which is used in the manufacturing process and we hold that Hydrazene 100% is also eligible for the benefit of MODVAT Credit. In view of above, we find no merits in the appeal of the Revenue and therefore we reject the same."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Assessee, a manufacturer, was availing modvat credit under rule 57A - Modvat credit was denied to assessee on a ground that it had taken Modvat credit on strength of original copies of invoice without taking/applying for permission from competent authority under rule 57G(2A) - Tribunal, in view of finding recorded by Commissioner that there was no dispute regarding duty paid character of inputs and their receipt/utilization in manufacture of final product, held that requisite twin conditions contemplated in rule 57G(6) were satisfied and hence modvat credit taken on original invoice was admissible - Whether, no substantial question of law arose from order of Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 8 to 11] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 23/94-CE (N.T.), dated 20-5-1994; Trade Notice dated 23-5-1994 issued by Chandigarh Collectorate

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of carbon black. It was availing the facility of modvat credit under rule 57A. On scrutiny of RT-12 returns, filed by the assessee, it was noticed that the assessee had taken modvat credit on the strength of original copies of invoices without taking/applying for permission from the competent authority under rule 57G(2A). Hence, the adjudicating authority disallowed the modvat credit and confirmed the demands under rule 57-I along with penalties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) remanded the matter to adjudicating authority for de novo proceedings. In remand proceedings, the adjudicating authority allowed the modvat credit, holding that there was no dispute regarding the duty paid character of the inputs and their receipt/utilization in manufacture of final product. Being aggrieved, the revenue successfully took the matter in appeals to the Commissioner against which assessee preferred appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed.

On appeal :

HELD: The question whether a statutory provision is mandatory or directory depends upon the intent of the Legislature and not upon the language in which the intent is clothed. It needs little emphasis that all parts of the statute or sections have to be construed together with reference to the context, so that construction put on a particular provision makes it consistent with the enactment and does not lead a manifestly absurd result not intended by the Legislature. A literal construction which makes a particular provision manifestly absurd or leads to anomalous results is to be avoided. [Para 8]

From a conjoint reading of sub-rules (3) and (6), of rule 57G, the intent and object of the Legislature is manifestly clear. It is to prevent the misuse of the modvat claims and any fraud being played by a manufacturer. Being a beneficial legislation, its object of input duty relief to a manufacturer should not be defeated on a technical and strict interpretation of the Rules governing modvat. In fact, in order to obviate any difficulty on account of loss of duplicate copy of the invoices, Notification No. 23/94-CE. (N.T.), dated 20-5-1994 has been issued by the Board enabling a manufacturer to take Modvat credit on the basis of original copy of the invoice, provided the loss of duplicate copy of the invoice had occurred only in transit and the Assistant Commissioner is satisfied about its loss. [Para 9]

In the instant case, while holding that the assessee was entitled to take modvat credit on the basis of original invoice, the Tribunal had relied on a Trade Notice issued by the Chandigarh Collectorate, dated 23-5-1994, wherein it has been provided that an assessee could take credit on the basis of original invoice, subject to the satisfaction of the jurisdictional Assistant Collector. The Tribunal had held that in view of the finding recorded by the Commissioner to the effect that there was no dispute regarding the duty-paid character of the inputs and their receipt/utilisation in the manufacture of final product, the requisite twin conditions contemplated in sub-rule (6), the modvat credit taken on original invoices was admissible. [Para 10]

In view of the aforesaid concurrent findings of fact recorded by the two appellate authorities below, modvat credit could not be denied to the assessee on merits. In this view of the matter, the question proposed by the revenue was rendered academic and could not be said to be a substantial question of law. [Para 11]

Resultantly, the appeals were to be dismissed. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit

HELD: Modvat - Denial not sustainable where non-levy was not due to default by input manufacturer and proper records were kept. ".......where the initial non-levy was not due to any default or irregularity on the part of the manufacturer and duty is recovered later on by the department, it will be totally iniquitous to deny the benefit of modvat, particularly where the records maintained are amenable to scrutiny and verification."

notwithstanding any right arising as a consequence to such payment. [Para 16]

It is important to understand the structure of various taxes, duties, cess and fees which have bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation. There are broadly two categories of taxes, duties, cess and fees based on chargeability prevalent in India having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods as under: First category of the taxes, duties, cess and fees having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are those which are to be absorbed by the enterprise as part of the component of its costs as per prevailing relevant laws, rules and regulations, without any benefit granted by law of adjusting these taxes, duties, cess and fees against the final excise duty payable on the finished goods manufactured by the enterprise. For example, Custom duty payable on import of raw materials broadly has three elements of duties apart from education and secondary education cess viz. (a) Basic Custom Duty (b) Counter veiling Duty (CVD) (c) Special Additional duties(SAD). The basic custom duty paid on import of raw materials for manufacture of finished goods is not allowed as a credit of taxes to be set off against the excise duty payable on the finished goods manufactured by the enterprises under the current value added tax regime known as Cenvat credit scheme and hence is to be absorbed as cost component by the enterprise while in the case of the CVD & SAD component in custom duty paid by the enterprise on import of raw materials for manufacture of finished goods, the same are allowed as Cenvat credit to be set off/utilized for payment of excise duty on the finished goods. Similarly, Central Sales Tax(CST) paid on purchase of raw material from another state, no offset is allowed against the State VAT or CST on finished goods sold by the enterprise as per current schemes pertaining to sales tax and hence is to be absorbed as part of component of cost by the enterprise while State VAT paid on purchase of raw material from supplier within the State is allowed to be set-off against the VAT/CST payable on sale of finished goods to avoid cascading effect of taxes. [Para 16]

The second categories of taxes, duties, cess and fees having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are known as 'Value Added Taxes'-These Value added taxes were introduced in India in 1986 to avoid cascading effect of taxes with an objective to reduce transaction cost and bring transparency in the system. The scheme allowed setting off of duties paid on procurement of inputs against the duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise thereby restricting the levy of tax to value addition done by the enterprise in manufacturing the finished goods. The scheme when launched in 1986 was called Modified Value Added tax scheme (popularly known as MODVAT scheme) which allowed credit/set off of duties paid on specified inputs used in manufacture of excisable goods against the excise duty liability of the enterprise on manufacture of goods as per provisions of Excise Laws, rules and regulations. The scheme was expanded and credit of duty paid on capital goods was also brought under the ambit of the scheme MODVAT in the year 1994. The scheme was later renamed CENVAT Credit scheme in the year 2000. The 'Service Tax' was introduced in India from the year 1994 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 were introduced in the year 2002 to allow credit on input services used in providing taxable output services. In the year 2004, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 were unified and new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were introduced. The new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 allowed both manufacturers and service providers to take input credit on goods and services apart from capital goods allowing cross sectorial availment and utilization of credit. The Cenvat Credit Rules permit adjustment of excise duties paid on inputs, CVD/SAD on imports of raw material, excise duties on capital goods and service tax on input services against the excise duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise without one to one co-relation required by the enterprise to establish before availing the Cenvat credit. The Central Government has now announced its intention to introduce unified Goods and Service Tax, popularly known as 'GST' which is likely to be rolled out shortly which is likely to further unify and merge various indirect taxes both Central and State levies into an unified tax to be known as 'GST' and allow credit of various indirect taxes across goods and services both Central and State levies as per scheme to be notified which will further help in cutting down transaction costs and bring in transparency into the system. [Para 16]

facts.text: The issue to be determined in this Revenue appeal is whether, in order to avail Modvat credit, it is mandatory to specifically mention the inputs in the declaration filed under Rule 57G of Central Excise Rules, 1944 or it is sufficient to mention the Tariff heading under which these items are classified.

Besides manufacturing chlorine, the appellant company also manufactures hydrochloric acid, essential for the treatment of effluents generated during the process of manufacture of chlorine. The appellants claimed Modvat credit under Rule 57A on hydrochloric acid in terms of Notfn. 217/86-CE, as hydrochloric acid used has to be considered as an input for the finished product (chlorine).

The assessee claimed Modvat credit of the duty paid on inputs on the basis of original copies of invoices under rule 57G. The adjudicating authority disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that under rules 52A and 57G, the Modvat credit could be claimed on the basis of the duplicate copy of invoice and not on the basis of the original invoice and, therefore, the claim of the Modvat credit was in violation of rules 52A and 57G. He further held that the assessee had wrongly availed the benefit of rule 57G(2A) and despite sufficient time given to it to produce the required duty paying documents, the same were not produced.

Both, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. The Tribunal also refused to entertain the plea of the assessee that the duplicate copy (transporter’s copy) of the invoice had been lost in the transit and the matter might be remanded to the adjudicating authority for the consideration of the aforesaid explanation saying that no such plea had been taken by the assessee before the adjudicating authority.

On application to the High Court :

The applicant, an importer of chemicals is a company having its Head Office at Mumbai and a Branch in Gujarat-Gandhidham, both the offices being registered under the GST Laws.

The applicants are wanting to import the chemicals at Halida Port (Kolkata, West Bengal) on their own but with Mumbai Head Office GSTIN. After import the goods will be stored at the rented Customs Bonded warehouse at Haldia Port. They do not have any establishment or place of operation or any godown or GSTIN in the State of West Bengal and after importation, want to clear the goods from that warehouse (Ex Bond) in the name of their Mumbai Head Office. They want to sell such imported goods to customers in West Bengal and other States nearby from that warehouse and charge IGST by raising bills/invoices from Mumbai and not from West Bengal.

The terms of delivery will be ex-terminal (i.e., the ownership and its respective risks and rewards will be transferred to their customer the moment goods are cleared from the customs port). The goods will be transported directly from that port to customers in Kolkata or in any other states. The Tax Invoice will be raised from Mumbai Head Office with Mumbai GSTIN levying IGST.

The applicant, is seeking an advance ruling in respect of the issue as to whether the procedure to raise the invoice from Mumbai Head Office for imports received at Haldia Port Kolkata where they do not have any separate GST Registration and Charge IGST from Mumbai to their customers is correct? or do they have to take separate registration in the State of West Bengal for the transactions and if they do not need separate registration in West Bengal, can they do the transaction on Mumbai Head Office GSTIN, then in case of issuance of e-way bill is it correct to mention the GSTIN of Mumbai and Dispatch place of Haldia Port?

The assessee-job worker manufactured wet grinder for company EUAL out of the raw material supplied by EUAL under cover of invoice issued under rule 57G. On the basis of the said invoice issued, the assessee availed Modvat credit. However, the department took the view that no ‘sale’ was involved in supply of goods to assessee by EUAL and, therefore, the invoices were not valid documents for the purpose of availment of Modvat on those goods. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the entitlement of Modvat credit to the assessee.

On appeal:

The assessee engaged in the manufacture of cold rolled steel strips was availing Modvat credit facility in respect of duty paid on the inputs. Modvat credit was disallowed to the assessee on ground that it had taken Modvat credit on the strength of the carbon copy of challans issued by input supplier (TISCO). According to the revenue under rule 57G, Modvat credit was permissible only when the inputs were accompanied by original duty payment documents. The assessee’s appeal against said disallowance was dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals). The Tribunal also dismissed assessee’s appeal.

On reference :

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture and sale of aluminium products. The Assistant Commissioner, denied Modvat credit on inputs on the grounds that the words 'duplicate invoice' was not mentioned and in one invoice, the portion showing the words 'original and duplicate' was torn and according to Rule 57G as it stood during the relevant period, Modvat credit could have been allowed only on furnishing of duplicate invoice and not otherwise. The Commissioner (Appeals) had also upheld the disallowance of Modvat credit. However, the Tribunal had held that after the amendment of Rule 57G vide Notification No. 7/99-CE(NT), dated 9th February, 1999 the credit cannot be denied on minor procedural lapses in case the inputs were duty paid and further in view of Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 that amendment would apply to all pending cases. The Tribunal, accordingly, held that assessee was entitled for the benefit of Modat credit in respect of the impugned inputs.

On appeal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of carbon black. It was availing the facility of modvat credit under rule 57A. On scrutiny of RT-12 returns, filed by the assessee, it was noticed that the assessee had taken modvat credit on the strength of original copies of invoices without taking/applying for permission from the competent authority under rule 57G(2A). Hence, the adjudicating authority disallowed the modvat credit and confirmed the demands under rule 57-I along with penalties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) remanded the matter to adjudicating authority for de novo proceedings. In remand proceedings, the adjudicating authority allowed the modvat credit, holding that there was no dispute regarding the duty paid character of the inputs and their receipt/utilization in manufacture of final product. Being aggrieved, the revenue successfully took the matter in appeals to the Commissioner against which assessee preferred appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed.

On appeal :

Iron & Steel products are manufactured by the appellants. They filed a declaration under Rule 57G of CE Rules for availing MODVAT benefit in respect of inputs used in relation to their manufacture of finished products. The Assistant Collector held that the refractory products are not covered by the explanation in Rule 57A of CE Rules. This order was upheld by Collector (Appeal).

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

It availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it was capital goods in terms of rule 57Q.

The lower authorities including the Tribunal disallowed the Modvat credit.

On appeal to High Court:

Without filing a declaration under Rule 57G, CER, the respondents were paying duty on the final product "Cables complete" through RG-23A, Part II, by utilising Modvat credit taken on the input, cables. The product was, however, being made through job workers with the permission taken under Rule 57F(2). Classification lists and price lists filed. The department held that in the absence of declaration under Rule 57G, duty could be paid only through PLA or in cash and not through RG-23A Demands were therefore raised taking the clearances as made without payment of proper duty.

The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

• The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of writing and printing paper.

• Their head office was registered as input service distributor.

• The assessee availed the credit of Rs.5,70,423 on consultancy services used for modemisation of their power plant as a measure of increasing efficiency and profitability of their plant; as a result of such services, the cost of power was reduced.

• The assessee had entered into agreement with a foreign party for C.D.M. Emission Reduction known as Clean Development Reductions for additional earning in terms of Certified Emission Reduction Sale (CERS) of Carbon. The additional earning was available if a company had or was to install project of high technical equipments in power plant, in which fossil fuel like rice husk etc. were used, which reduced carbon emission.

• The assessee were already having a power plant in which rice husk was used as fuel resultantly the carbon emission was reduced. For having such type of plant the appellants were entitled to get additional earning on CERS. For earning the said amount of CERS of about Rs. 4.8 crores, they availed consultancy services of which CENVAT credit was taken by the assessee through their head office.

• The Department denied credit of such services contending that they were used for the project of Certified Emission Reduction Sale of Carbon which was neither dutiable nor taxable.

Issue involved

• Whether the assessee was entitled to credit ?

The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

After fulfilling all the requirements, the appellants had taken Modvat credit in respect of Oleum, used in the manufacture of OSAA detergent. In the process of manufacture only 49% of the Oleum put in the manufacturing stream is actually consumed and the remaining portion emerges as spent acid (which was declared in the classification list and allowed by the authorities to be cleared without payment of duty). Limiting Modvat credit to the extent the Oleum is actually consumed, the Additional Collector of Central Excise reversed the Modvat credit as having been wrongly availed in respect of the remaining amount and demanded a duty of Rs. 2,71,024.77 under Rule 57F read with Rule 9(2), Central Excise Rules, 1944. Aggrieved by the above order, the appellants have come in appeal.

The assessee had set up a petrochemical complex for manufacture of naphtha based on petrochemical products.

For the purpose of meeting its requirement of electricity and steam, a power plant was set up by the assessee in a joint venture with HPLCL and power agreement for a period of 20 years was signed between the assessee and HPLCL. In terms of this agreement, the assessee was required to supply Naptha, as such, or partially processed Naphtha (CLP) and start up fuel free of cost to HPLCL through pipeline for generation of electricity and steam, which would be returned to the assessee for use in the manufacture of its final products. As per the terms of the power agreement, the assessee was required to pay conversion charges to HPLCL for carrying out the aforesaid operation. The land on which the power plant was situated had been assigned by the assessee to HPLCL for a period of 20 years. The power plant was situated within the factory complex. Cenvat credit would be available on naphta used as input for generation of electricity. The Superintendent informed the assessee that Cenvat credit on Naptha used for generation of electricity and steam by the power plant would not be allowed.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the power plant was under the ownership of a different company, HPLCL, and the land on which the power plant was situated was assigned by the assessee to HPLCL by way of a deed of assignment and, as such, it no more remained the part of the factory premises of the assessee; that the factory of the assessee and the power plant of HPLCL were in two separate premises; that the Modvat credit was permissible only in respect of the duty paid on the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used for manufacture of the final product or for any other purpose within the factory of production; and that since the input was being used for generation of electricity or steam outside the factory of production, Modvat credit was not available.

Thereafter, the Commissioner issued a show-cause notice to the assessee raising duty demand.

On second appeal:

Facts [Hindustan Zinc]

In case of Hindustan Zinc Ltd., assessee obtained zinc ore concentrate [Zinc Sulphide (ZnS)] from the mines on payment of excise duty which is used as an input for the production of zinc.

When ZnS is heated (calcined) at high temperature in the presence of oxygen, zinc oxide (ZnO) and sulphuric acid are produced.

Zinc Oxide is further oxidised to produce zinc.

Sulphur obtained as a technological necessity is a pollutant and is, therefore, converted into sulphur dioxide in the presence of catalysts like Vanadium Pentaoxide & Hydrogen Peroxide. Sulphuric acid is converted into sulphur and the assessee did not take any Cenvat Credit on the inputs used after the emergence of sulphur dioxide.

The sulphuric acid produced as a by-product is sold on payment of excise duty to various industries.

In some cases, sulphuric acid was sold under exemption for use in/as fertilizers.

The Department argued that as per rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 (Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004), the assessee was obliged to maintain separate accounts and records for the inputs used in the production of zinc and sulphuric acid and in the absence of the same the assessee was obliged to pay 8% as an amount on the sale price of exempt sulphuric acid.

The assessee argued that the very purpose of the grant of exemption to sulphuric acid was to keep the input costs at the lowest for the production of fertilizers during the relevant period. Fertilizers themselves were wholly exempted from the payment of excise duty because the government wanted the farmgate price to the farmer should be at the lowest. In fact, the government grants subsidies to the fertilizer plants for the difference between the cost of production and sale price determined by the government. Any duty demand on the sulphuric acid will defeat the very purpose of grant of exemption and make the fertilizer cost higher than the desirable level. In such a scenario, such higher cost will have to be compensated by the government as subsidy.

The assessee challenged the show cause notices by filing writ petitions under article 226 before the Rajasthan High Court, primarily challenging the vires of rule 57CC on the ground that the Central Government by subordinate legislation, can not fix rates of duties which is the prerogative of the Parliament under section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with Central Excise Tariff Act, 1975. As an alternative, it was pleaded that even if rule 57 CC is to be held as intra vires, the demand raised in the show cause notices will not survive on proper interpretation of rule 57CC of the Rules and hence is to be quashed.

The High Court decided the petition in favour of the assessee on the interpretation of rule 57CC and rule 57D itself, without going into question relating to vires.

Revenue argued that merely a show cause notice was issued and no final decision was taken on the said show cause notice. However, instead of showing cause, writ petitions were filed seeking quashing of the show cause notice which should have been dismissed as premature. Hence, High Court should not have entertained writ petition questioning the validity of the show cause notice.

Facts [Rallis India]
