Per Justice Shri U.L. Bhat, President :

Appellant, M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd., Bombay with Head Office at Bombay has a factory in Aligarh for manufacture of Complan and other nutrients. Appellant was availing Modvat credit on certain inputs. The dispute arose on scrutiny of monthly RT 12 Return for October 94. Various items of Modvat were objected to. After hearing the appellant, the objection regarding Rs. 53,309 being the duty element of the input covered by Invoice Nos. 1062, 1075 and 1081 issued by the manufacturer was confirmed and corresponding amount of duty demanded, though other objections were dropped. Confirmation of the demand by the Assistant Commissioner having been confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), the present appeal has been filed.

2. Copies of three invoices in question are before me. They were issued by the manufacturer of inputs to M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Bombay. In the column against destination, Aligarh is seen mentioned. The case of the appellant that order for the input was placed by the Head Office at Bombay for use at the factory in Aligarh is not denied by the Department. The lower authorities objected to the admissibility of Modvat credit on the ground that the invoices were endorsed by the Head Office in favour of factory. Being governed by the Central Excise Rules, 1944, central excise licence was taken in respect of the Aligarh factory in the name of Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Aligarh. This does not mean that there are two different companies called M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Aligarh. There is only one entity M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Bombay with head office at Bombay and this company has factory at several places including the factory at Aligarh. It is evident from the invoices that order was placed by the Head Office at Bombay for supply to and use in the Aligarh unit. That being so, it cannot be said that there is endorsement on the invoices by one entity to another. The expression "endorsement" has been used only loosely in this context. This is not a case of transfer of inputs by one legal entity to a third party. This is a case where supply had been arranged by Head Office for the use of the factory.

There can be no legal objection to the availment of Modvat credit on the basis of invoices issued in the name of the company at its registered Head Office, though used in the factory at Aligarh. This view is supported by the decisions of the Tribunal in the cases of Larsen Toubro Ltd. 1994 (72) ELT 948 (T), Bansal Containers (P) Ltd. 1994 (3) RLT 215(CEGAT) = 1996 (83) ELT 425 (T), Siyaram Platex (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 915 (T) and Snow Cem India Ltd. 1994 (4) RLT 119 (CEGAT) = 1997 (96) ELT 627 (T).

3. In this view, the appellant was entitled to avail Modvat credit on the basis of the invoices referred to above.

4. The impugned orders are set aside and the appeal is allowed.

1. M/s. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Limited, 3203, GIDC Estate, Bharuch, Anklcshwar, Gujarat -393002 [for short - 'applicant'} is registered under GST and their GSTIN is 24AAACC6251E1Z5.

The Applicant is a public limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 and is inter alia engaged in the manufacture and supply of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API). In order to enhance their operational efficiency and cost optimization, they arc setting up a Solvent Recovery Plant ("SRP") for recycling solvents and a Mobile Effluent Treatment Plant ("METP") for treatment and disposal of wastewater used in various stages of API production. In order to carry out the construction work of the SRP & METP plant, the Applicant has issued various Purchase Orders to three suppliers namely Uma Infra Project Co., Parth Construction and Kirti Infrastructure Ltd.

3. The SRP typically utilizes distillation, adsorption or 2.5 membrane separation processes to reclaim solvents from waste streams, enabling reuse and reducing environmental impact. The detailed process is as under: -

•

During production: The Applicant uses multiple solvents and upon completion of these processes, a resultant Spent Solution is generated which comprises of residual solvent mixed with other chemical substances.

•

Spent Solution: The spent solution can neither be reused directly due to the presence of impurities that may compromise product quality, nor can it be disposed of directly as it contains valuable recoverable material and may pose environmental and regulatory concerns.

•

Recovery of usable solvent: The spent solution is subjected to a controlled distillation process within the SRP. The solution is heated to temperatures close to the solvent's boiling point, causing the solvent to vaporize. The vaporized solvent is passed through a condenser where it is cooled and converted back into liquid form.

•

Outcome: The recovered solvent is free from contaminants and suitable for re-use in production and the separated impurities are handled and disposed of as per environmental regulations.

•

Recovered Solvent: It is collected in designated storage tanks and transferred through pumps to the manufacturing units as per production requirements.

4. As the solvent recovery process involves a highly controlled and regulated process to ensure quality, efficacy, and safety, the following equipment will be installed inside the SRP plant, namely: -

•

Reactor: It is used for flash distillation of spent solvent. The reactor rapidly heats the spent solvent mixture, causing the volatile solvent component to vaporize quickly while the heavier residues remain.

•

Kcttlcs/Rcboiler/Distillation columns: These equipments are used for fractional distillation of spent solvents. The Kettles/Reboilers provide the heat source for distillation, ensuring consistent vapor generation whereas distillation columns facilitate the separation of solvent mixtures based on differing boiling points.

•

Phase separators: It is used to separate immiscible liquid phases based on density differences, such as sol vent-water or solvent-organic impurities. Often used after condensation and before distillation to ensure efficient separation. It clears separation of solvent for recovery and water/effluent for treatment.

•

Heat Exchangers: It facilitates temperature control during various stages of the SRP process and ensures optimal energy usage. It is used to pre-heat spent solvents before distillation and to cool recovered solvent vapors postdistillation.

•

Storage Tanks/ Intermediate Receivers: These tanks help to segregate solvents by grade, batch or recovery stage and provide temporary or long-term storage of solvents at various stages. Its essential function is to store spent insolvents before processing, hold intermediate solvent fractions postdistillation and collect recovered solvents ready for reuse in API manufacturing.

•

Centrifugal Pumps: It handles the transfer of liquid throughout the plant and facilitates seamless, closed-loop solvent handling to avoid manual exposure and contamination.

•

Brine Chiller: It provides deep chilling for low temperature solvent consideration. It uses brine solution as a coolant to achieve temperatures lower than water-based chilling systems.

•

Water Chiller: It cools down process solvents or effluent before phase separation or storage and is generally used for standard chilling requirements in the SRP system.

•

Cooling Towers: These cooling towers act as a support system for distillation and heat exchange operations as it provides general purpose cooling for utilities in the SRP system by circulating cooling water used in heat exchangers and condensers.

VI. Modvat credit of Rs. 72,97,835/- of duty paid on inputs not received in the factory premises of the appellants:

According to the Department, records show that all inputs namely acrylic scrap was received at the appellants Head office located at D/19, SMA Cooperative, GT Karnal Road, Delhi from where the same was transported in small quantities to the factory without accounting for the same. The Department alleges that credit had been availed on the basis of duty paying documents only, without physical receipt of inputs at the place of manufacture and that they have not obtained any permission from the Excise authorities for storing inputs at a place other than within their factory. However, it is the case of the appellants that they received all the inputs within their factory under cover of bills of entry but they have failed to explain as to why challans showing receipt of inputs from their Head office at later dates were issued or as to which inputs were received on these challans. They have not produced any evidence to show that the entire quantity of inputs on which the above mentioned scrap was taken, were actually received inside their factory. The bills of entry relied upon by the appellants will not answer this question as the bills of entry would only show that inputs were imported by the appellants. The Department does not dispute import of acrylic scrap by the appellants but disputes receipt of the imported goods within the factory for manufacture of final products. The plea of the assessee that the goods were shifted from the head office to the factory under cover of transport documents which are now available with them, cannot be considered at this belated stage. The charge in the show cause notice regarding wrong availment of this amount of credit is very clear. The allegation in the show cause notice is reproduced below :

"In regard to the inputs found short, scrutiny of documents appear to have revealed that the assessee had been availing the credit on the basis of documents only without fulfilling requirements of Rule 57-G of Central Excise Rules, 1944 according to which no credit shall be taken by the manufacturer unless the inputs are received in the factory under the cover of an invoice issued under Rule 520A or 100% EOU or Bill of entry. It is further noticed that in this case the assessee had neither taken the Commissioner's permission for storage of the inputs at the place other than the factory and to bring inputs from such storage point to their factory for the purpose of availing modvat credit. Shri Sanjay Aggarwal in his statement recorded on 15.6.97 admitted about the fact that they neither got any permission for such storage nor did they intimate the CE authorities about the storage of raw materials at a place other than the factory. Scrutiny of the records revealed that during the period 1995-96 to 1997-98, the party received 17,31,444 kgs. of raw materials at D-19, SMA Delhi as per details in the Annexure C to this notice and availed modvat credit against the documents at their factory at Sonepat"

If the assessees' submission is that goods although initially stored at their Head office were actually transported to their factory to be used in or in relation to the manufacture of plastic sheets, (their final product) they should have produced necessary evidence in the form of transport documents before the Adjudicating Authority. Not having done so, and not offering any explanation for non-submission of available transport documents, and in the absence of any application to bring on record additional evidence in the form of transport documents, they cannot be permitted to rely upon such evidence at this stage. Further the plea that during the year 1995-96, 5,93,712 kgs. of inputs were directly received in their factory at Sonepat, as seen from the bills of entry and modvat credit of Rs. 22,67,959/- has been rightly availed against the invoices covering this quantity, has also not been raised by the appellants before the Commissioner and therefore, they cannot be heard on this plea at this late stage. We therefore, uphold the finding that the appellants availed in-admissible credit of Rs. 72,97,835/- in contravention of Rule 57-A and 57-G of the Central Excise Rules.

The Supreme Court in its landmark judgment in the case of Swadeshi Polytex Limited vs. Collector of Central Excise 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC) was pleased to hold as follows :

This was a decision rendered under the proforma regime (set off duty on inputs) wherein provision similar to Rule 57D which permits retention of modvat credit on inputs even if the same is used in the manufacture of dutiable final products and emergence of by-products, waste or refuse is not to be denied.

Para 20

"It is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible.

2. SCENARIO UNDER THE MODVAT REGIME BETWEEN 01/03/86 TO 03/09/94

Bearing the spirit of the decision of the Supreme Court in Swadeshi Polytex the lawmakers when they introduced Modvat Scheme, brought into force a specific provision in the form of Rule 57D(1) of the Central Excise Rules which reads as under :

Credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs shall not be denied or varied on the ground that part of the inputs is contained in any waste, refuse or by product arising during the manufacture of the final product, whether or not such waste, refuse or by product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty or is not specified as a final product under Rule 57A.

WHILE INTRODUCING RULE 57D CENTRAL GOVT ALSO BROUGHT INTO FORCE RULE 57C WHICH READS AS UNDER :

Credit to duty not to be allowed if final products are exempt. No credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty.

Rule 57G of the said rule of 1944 provided for procedure to be observed by the manufacturer enabling the manufacturer intending to take credit of the duty paid on inputs under Rule 57A to file a declaration as contemplated under sub-rule (1) and take credit of the duty on the inputs received by him under sub-rule (2). The necessary procedural safeguards were also provided under Rule 57G by laying down in sub-rule (3) (c) that no such credit shall be taken unless the inputs were received in the factory under the cover of any of the documents enumerated thereunder. When the goods were seized within the period of limitation prescribed under sub-rule (5) for taking credit, the manufacturer could not have exercised his right to take modvat credit on the strength of the invoice because the goods could not be received in the factory under that document for no fault on the part of the assessee. Even if the assessee was issued invoice dated 28.9.97 for the goods to be received in his factory, it was impossible for the assessee to do so, since they were seized. The period of limitation of six months as contemplated in sub-rule (5) of Rule 57G is not intended to apply to such cases where it becomes impossible for the assessee to receive the goods in the factory under the invoice by virtue of seizure made while the goods were in transit. The very fact that the goods were in transit on the same date i.e. 28.9.97 under the invoice to the factory address of the assessee would show that, ordinarily the goods would have been received in the factory of the assessee around that date and much before the expiry of the period of six months. Therefore, sub-rule (5) of Rule 57G cannot be enforced in cases where the assessee's right to receive the goods in the factory under an invoice as contemplated by sub-rule (2) and (3) cannot be exercised due to the hurdle created by the department by way of seizure of goods which was later on released after the said six month's period. Once the goods were released, the assessee was in a position to receive the goods in its factory, and they were so received on 10.4.98. Therefore, respectfully following the ratio of the decisions of the Tribunal in Phoenix Industries Ltd. and Natraj Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (supra) which followed the larger bench judgment in Kusum Ingots and Alloys Ltd. (supra), it is hereby held, that the impugned orders denying the modvat credit to the assessee on the ground that it was taken after the prescribed period of six months can not be sustained. The impugned orders are hereby set aside with the consequential relief to the appellant. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules stipulates that inputs are to be received under the cover of a gate pass, an AR-I, a Bill of Entry or any other document as may be prescribed by the Board. Gate pass is a document prescribed for removal of the goods from the factory of manufacturer to the first destination. This is evident from the provisions of Rule 52A and Rule 173G of the Central Excise Rules. Hence, when there is a stipulation in Rule 57G that the inputs are to be received under gate pass by the claimant of modvat credit, it should be normally taken to mean that the said Rule contemplates receipt of inputs straight from the factory of manufacturer under gate pass. In that case, the consignee is necessarily to be the modvat claimant and consignor being the manufacturer of inputs, However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the case of Small Scale Units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement, by permitting one endorsement in the gate passes initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting up to two endorsements in the gate passes. This relaxation made by the Board appears to be purely of administrative nature based on consideration of implementing the modvat scheme, so long as the duty paid nature of the goods and duty paid thereon could be established. As seen from the Trade Notice cited by the learned Advocate, it is evident that the Government is keen to extend the modvat credit so long as the goods in factory packed condition as are covered by the gate passes are received by the parties intending to avail modvat credit. Going by this spirit of the relaxation, we are unable appreciate the routine and mechanical approach of the authorities below in rejecting the claim of the modvat credit only on the ground that more than one endorsement have been made. When the Board themselves have taken a decision to relax the procedural requirement by way of administrative instruction it should be the endeavour of the authorities to extend modvat credit wherever, the duty paid nature of the goods is evident from the gate passes produced and quantum of duty paid on the inputs could be ascertained from them. A positive approach is called for in this regard. We also take note of the argument of Shri Arya that permitting a number of endorsements would involve in considerable administrative burden and the gate passes are likely to be abused. In this case, it is contended by the other side that the previous endorsements have been made not by any other manufacturer who could utilise this inputs but only by intermediaries in the trade channel. In any case, the department is entitled to make verification or investigation with regard to the genuineness of the gate pass and also the question whether gate pass has been utilised for availment of modvat credit at the earliest stages. In this case, no such enquiry appears to have been conducted and the modvat credit has been denied only on the ground that more than that of permitted endorsements have been made in the gate passes. Such an order cannot be sustainable in the context of the scheme of modvat credit read along with the relaxation made by the Board."

The date of issue of the documents has to be excluded for the purpose of counting the 6 months period as held in Punjab Breweries Ltd.'s case (Supra). Accordingly, Modvat Credit is available to them. In respect of availment of credit on the strength of Bills of Entry in the name of Head Office the Central Board of Excise & Customs itself has allowed the availment of credit provided the Head Office endorses the Bill of Entry in the name of the manufacturing unit. The Modvat credit has been disallowed by not accepting the said invoice on the ground that the same shows the address of their head office instead of the factory and there is no endorsement by the head office. Further the department has also doubted the actual receipt of the goods in their factory premises because the applicants have failed to produce any documents showing the actual receipt and [since] the transporters' column in the invoices [having been]left blank. However, I find that the applicants have explained before the Assistant Commissioner, vide their reply to the show cause notice, that the input in question was transported personally by one of their employees in asmuchas the same was only 115.3 K.gs. of stainless steel wire for which a regular transport was not required. They had also produced the good's receipt report. I have seen the photocopy of the report produced on record. The same is carrying a printed serial number and is duly signed by their store-keeper. I also find that the cardex maintained by them reflects the receipt of the above material. Further, there is no dispute or doubt about the fact that the said material was duly entered in their RG-23A Part-I record. Having entered the goods in their Modvatable raw material register, the applicants could not have escaped to show the utilisation of the same in the manufacture of final product and to clear the final product on payment of duty. It is not a case where the applicants have availed the Modvat credit in their Part-II register without the corresponding receipt of raw material in their part I register. As such I find that the failure on the part of the applicants to show the transporters' mode in the invoice, to take the goods first to their head office, got the invoice endorsed in their factory and then transport the goods to their factory are no reasons for denial of benefit of Modvat credit to them. Endorsement of the invoice by their own head office is a rectifiable defect in any case. Taking all these issues into consideration I hold that the applicants had made out a prima facie case for granting them unconditional stay. I Order accordingly.

5. As only above points are involved in the appeal, I take up the appeal itself and allow the same. The impugned order is set aside.

Per Jyoti Balasundaram : The Revenue is aggrieved by the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) who has held that modvat credit is available to the respondents herein on invoices not containing all the requisite particulars as prescribed in Trade Notice No. 51/94 dated 27.7.94 read with Rule 57GG of the Central Excise Rules. On hearing both sides and perusing the show cause notice issued to the respondents herein, I agree that the notice does not spell out the grounds for denial of credit and the grounds have been spelt out in the first time only in the memorandum of appeal viz. credit is not available since the invoice did not contain particulars such as name, address and registration number of factory/warehouse, date and time of removal of goods etc. Further, I find that the Commissioner (Appeals) has satisfied himself on the basic requirement such as payment of duty on the inputs covered by the invoice, receipt of the same in the factory of the respondents and utilisation thereof in the final products manufactured by the respondents. Rule 57GG prescribes that registered person has to issue invoices containing the details as prescribed by CBEC and the Trade Notice details which should be found on invoice. Since the duty paying nature of the inputs and the validity of the duty paying documents viz. invoice are not in dispute and further since inputs were received in original packing from the manufacturer to the factory premises of the respondents, there is no reason for denial of credit to the respondents herein. The respondents having substantially complied with the requirements prescribed under Rule 57GG, I uphold the impugned order extending modvat credit and reject the appeal.

Considered the submissions. I find that Notification No. 21/94 which was pressed into service by both the lower authorities for disallowing the modvat credit to the appellants ceased to have effect after 31.12.1994. The invoices in question were issued by the depot of the input-manufacturer in December 1995, when Notification No. 21/94 was not in force. Therefore, I find, the reliance placed by the lower authorities on Notification No. 21/94 for denying Modvat credit to the party by attributing invalidity to the invoices issued after 31.12.1994 is erroneous. Coming to Notification No. 32/94 relied on by the appellants, I find that, under this Notification, Govt. prescribed invoices issued by manufacturers from their depots as documents for purposes of Rule 57G. The explanation to this Notification states, inter alia, that "invoice" means a document issued by a registered person for sale of goods. Admittedly, the depot which issued the invoices in question had got itself registered prior to the date of issue of the invoices. Notification No. 32/94 was in force on the date of issue of those invoices and the same covered the appellants' case inasmuch as the invoices in question were issued by a registered person, which was the depot of the input-manufacturer.

5. The Trade Notice cited by ld. advocate has also been examined and I observe that, as per this Trade Notice, only the actual amount of duty paid in the manufacturer's invoice issued under Rule 52-A should be indicated in the invoice issued from their depot under Rule 57G, and not the duty payable on the value charged by the depot. Where the sale from the depot has been effected at a price higher than that shown in the Rule 52A invoice, the manufacturer after payment of differential duty can obtain a certificate under Rule 57E in order to facilitate the buyer to avail further Modvat credit. In the instant case, the appellants had produced the Rule 57E certificate (relating to payment of differential duty by the input-manufacturer) to the adjudicating authority, but the latter did not accept it on account of its having been issued after the date of issue of the depot's invoices. The lower appellate authority appears to have taken the same view. Both the authorities have held that the depot's invoices contained wrong information. I find that such a finding, recorded with reference to the Rule 57E certificate, is beyond the scope of the SCN. The appellants were entitled to Modvat credit of the full amount of duty of Rs. 79,847/- on the strength of the depot's invoices coupled with the certificate dated 4.1.96 issued under Rule 57E by the C.E. Superintendent, Bhandara (certifying payment of Rs. 69170/- towards differential duty of excise on the inputs in question by the input-manufacturer) inasmuch as the certificate itself was a document prescribed under Rule 57G (3) for the purpose of taking credit of duty.

6. In view of the findings recorded above, I set aside the impugned order and allow the appeal with consequential reliefs to the appellants.

PROFORMA FOR DECLARATION TO BE FILED UNDER RULE 57G FOR AVAILING CREDIT OF DUTY PAID ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57A

Per P.G. Chacko : This appeal is against denial of Modvat credit totalling to Rs. 96,795/- by the lower authorities. A part of this credit on inputs was taken on the strength of an invoice which was originally issued by the input-manufacturer to another unit of the appellant-company and subsequently endorsed by that unit to the appellant unit. The remaining credit was taken on the strength of six invoices issued by the input-manufacturer to the appellants. In respect of the single endorsed invoice aforesaid, the lower authorities held that the credit taken on the basis of such invoice was not admissible to the appellants as the endorsement of invoices was not permissible under Rule 57 G. In respect of the credit taken on the basis of the six invoices referred to above, it was held that those invoices were also not valid documents for Modvat credit purpose as the input manufacturer had apparently issued the invoices to another party [M/s. Aggarwal Gases, New Delhi] and the latter endorsed the invoices in favour of the appellants. The entire credit was accordingly, disallowed by the authorities. Hence this appeal.

2. Heard both sides.

3. Ld. counsel for the appellants submits that the invoice received by the appellants' Noida unit by mistake was just transmitted to their Ghaziabad unit (appellant-unit) with appropriate endorsement but without accompaniment of the goods which was received by the appellant-unit directly from the manufacturer. This kind of endorsement would not vitiate the validity of the invoice for Modvat Credit purpose under Rule 57 G. In this connection, reliance is placed on the Tribunal's decision in CCE, Coimbatore Vs. Coimbatore Murugan Mills [2003 (56) RLT 84], wherein it was held that, where inputs were transferred between two sister units of the company, there was no sale between the units and accordingly any endorsement on the invoice which accompanied the consignment would not invalidate the document for the purpose of Modvat credit being taken by another independent assessee who utilized the inputs. Referring to the other six invoices, counsel submits that all those invoices were issued by the input-manufacturers from their registered depot at New Delhi directly to the appellants. The only defect pointed out by the department in these invoices was that the name and address of another party (Aggarwal Gases) given under "customer name and address" had been scored of and the name and address of the appellant-unit was hand-written in each invoice. In each of these six invoices, the deletion of address of Aggarwal Gases was attested by the input manufacturers. Counsel submits that it is this attestation, which was mis-understood as endorsement by the department. As a matter of fact, none of these six invoices was an endorsed invoice within the meaning of this expression contemplated under Rule 57G. These invoices were regular invoices issued by the input manufacturer's depot in their capacity as a registered dealer and hence these document were valid for Modvat purpose under Rule 57G. In this respect also, counsel has cited certain decisions of the Tribunal. It is finally submitted that there is no dispute of the duty-paid nature of the inputs or of their utilization in the process of manufacture of final products in the appellant's factory. When the substantive conditions stood complied with, the authorities ought to have allowed the credit.

Tax credit

11. (1)(a) A registered dealer who has purchased the taxable goods (hereinafter referred to as the "purchasing dealer") shall be entitled to claim tax credit equal to the amount of,—

1[(i)

tax collected from the purchasing dealer, by a registered dealer from whom he has purchased such goods or the tax payable by the purchasing dealer to a registered dealer who has sold such goods to him during the tax period; or]

(ii)

tax paid by him during the tax period under 2[sub-section (1), (2), (5) or (6)] of 3[section 9; or]

4[(iii)

tax paid by the purchasing dealer under the Gujarat Tax on Entry of Specified Goods into Local Areas Act, 2001 (Guj. 22 of 2001);]

(b) The tax credit to be so claimed under this sub-section shall be subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2) to (12); and the tax credit shall be calculated in such manner as may be prescribed.

(2) The registered dealer who intends to claim the tax credit shall maintain the register and the books of accounts in such manner as may be prescribed.

(3) (a) Subject to the provisions of this section, tax credit to be claimed under sub-section (1) shall be allowed to a purchasing dealer on his purchase of taxable goods which are intended for the purpose of—

(i)

sale or re-sale by him in the State;

(ii)

sale in the course of inter-State trade and commerce;

(iii)

branch transfer or consignment of taxable goods to other States (subject to the provision of sub-clause (b) below);

(iv)

sales in the course of export out of the territory of India;

(v)

sales to export oriented units or the units in Special Economic Zones for sale in the course of export out of the territory of India;

(vi)

use as raw material in the manufacture of taxable goods intended for (i) to (v) above or in the packing of the goods so manufactured;

1[(vii)

use as capital goods meant for use in manufacture of taxable goods intended for (i) to (vi) above subject to the condition that such capital goods are purchased after the appointed day:]

Provided that if purchases are used partially for the purposes specified in this sub-section, the tax credit shall be allowed proportionate to the extent they are used for the purposes specified in this sub-section.

(b) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the amount of tax credit in respect of a dealer shall be reduced by the amount of tax calculated at the rate of four per cent 2[taxable on the turnover of purchases within the State]—

(i)

of taxable goods consigned or dispatched for branch transfer or to his agent outside the State; or

(ii)

of taxable goods which are used as raw materials in the manufacture or in the packing of goods which are dispatched outside the State in the course of branch transfer or consignment or to his agent outside the State,

1[(iii)

of fuels used for the manufacture of goods:]

3[Provided that where the rate of tax of the taxable goods consigned or dispatched by dealer for branch transfer or to his agent outside the State is less than four per cent, then the amount of tax credit in respect of such dealer shall be reduced by the amount of tax calculated at the rate of tax set out in the Schedule on such goods on the 4[taxable turnover of purchases within the State.]]

(4) The tax credit shall not be claimed by the purchasing dealer until the tax period in which he receives from a registered dealer from whom he has purchased taxable goods, a tax invoice (in original) containing particulars as may be specified under sub-section (1) of section 60 evidencing the amount of tax.

Input tax credit

21. (1) Subject to the provisions of the Act, for the purpose of calculating the net tax payable by a registered dealer for any tax period after being registered, an input tax credit as determined under this section shall be allowed to such registered dealer for the tax paid or payable in respect of all taxable sales other than the sales as may be prescribed, or purchases under section 14 during that period.

(2) The input tax credit to which the registered dealer is entitled to shall be the amount of tax paid by the registered dealer to the seller, on his turnover of purchases made during the tax period, intended to be used for the purposes and subject to the conditions as specified in sub-section (3), sub-section (4) and sub-section (5) and calculated in such manner as may be prescribed.

(3) Subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed, partial input tax credit may be allowed in such cases as may be notified by the Government.

(4) Input tax credit shall be allowed for purchase of goods made within the State from a registered dealer holding a valid certificate of registration and which are intended for the purpose of—

(a)

sale or resale by him in the State;

(b)

use as raw material or as capital goods in the manufacturing and processing of goods other than those exempt from tax under the Act intended for sale in the State;

(c)

sale in the course of inter-State trade and commerce;

(d)

sale in the course of export out of the territory of India; or

(e)

for use as containers for packing of goods other than those exempt from tax under the Act for sale or resale in the State :

Provided that in respect of transactions falling under clause (c), input tax credit may be allowed on the tax paid in excess of 4% on the raw materials used directly in the manufacture of the finished products :

Provided further that if purchases are used partially for the purposes specified in this sub-section, input tax credit shall be allowed proportionate to the extent they are used for the purposes specified in this sub-section:

Provided also that partial rebating shall be allowed where inputs are used in the following circumstances—

(i)

sales consisting of both taxable and exempted goods;

(ii)

sales consisting of sale and dispatches in the form of consignment and stock transfer to other States; and

(iii)

inputs are used for any other purpose in addition to use in the course of business.

(5) Input tax credit on capital goods shall be limited to plant and machinery directly connected with the manufacturing or processing of the finished products and input tax credit as admissible under this section shall commence from the date of commencement of commercial production or sale of taxable goods and shall be adjusted against tax payable on output over a period of three years in equal instalments with rebating allowed in every tax period:

Provided that in case of closure of business before the period specified in this sub-section, no further input tax credit shall be allowed and input tax credit carried forward, if any, shall be forfeited.

(6) Input tax credit shall be allowed in respect of inputs used in both taxable and non-taxable goods sent on stock or consignment transfer subject to the condition that tax paid in excess of 4% only shall be rebated.

(7) Input tax credit shall not be claimed by the dealer until the tax period in which he receives from the registered dealer from whom he has purchased the goods a tax invoice in the prescribed form (in original) evidencing the amount of tax (Input tax):

Provided that for good and sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing and in the prescribed manner, the Assessing Authority may allow such credit subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be specified. The set off, however, shall not be carried beyond the end of the second financial year.

(8) A registered dealer who intends to claim input tax credit under sub-section (1) shall, for the purpose of determining the amount of input tax credit, maintain accounts, and such other records as may be prescribed in respect of the purchases and sales made by him in the State.

(9) No input tax credit under sub-section (1) shall be claimed or be allowed to a registered dealer—

(i)

in respect of any taxable goods under the Act purchased by him from another registered dealer for resale but given away by way of free sample or gift;

(ii)

who is liable to turnover tax at a percentage of the turnover of sales, in lieu of tax, as provided under section 25;

(iii)

in respect of capital goods as specified in Schedule 'E';

(iv)

in respect of goods brought from outside the State against the tax paid in other States;

(v)

in respect of stock of goods remaining unsold at the time of closure of business;

. It may happen the recipient of input service may deduct some amount while paying to the service provider. For example, if the invoice is of Rs. 110.20, but the recipient of service (who is going to avail Cenvat credit) pays only Rs. 95 in full settlement of Bill, how much credit he can avail? By strict interpretation, no credit will be available as such a situation is not envisaged in the rules at all, though it is a practical reality. In such a case, reasonable course will be that Rs. 95 can be taken as price including service tax and then calculate service tax by back calculations. This would be in line with Explanation 2 to section 67 of Finance Act, 1994. It will be advisable to obtain credit note from person who had provided service, specifically showing service tax separately. If not possible, a debit note may be issued.

This may invite some problems and show-cause notices at lower level, but in view of ‘harmonious interpretation’ of provisions, this view should be held valid, at least at Tribunal level.

5.1 Rule of harmonious construction - In Jagdish Singh v. Lt. Governor [1997] AIR SCW 2106 = AIR 1997 SC 2239, it was observed -

"It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Further, a statute or a rule made thereunder should be read as a whole and one provision should be construed with reference to the other provision so as to make the rule consistent and any construction which would bring any inconsistency or repugnancy between one provision and the other should be avoided. One rule cannot be used to defeat another rule in the same Rules, unless it is impossible to effect harmonisation between them. - - A construction that reduces one of the provisions to a ‘dead letter’ is not a harmonious construction as one part is being destroyed and consequently, Court should avoid such construction". - similar views in British Airways Plc.v. UOI AIR 2002 SC 391 = 2001 AIR SCW 5197 = (2002) 2 SCC 95 = 139 ELT 6 (SC).

Parent company making payments and debiting amounts to group companies

6. In some cases, a group has common office. Many input services like rent, telephones, AMC of machines, insurance, etc., are common to all the group companies. Charges are paid by parent company and parent company debits the charges on proportionate basis to other group companies.

In such cases, as at present, there is no provision for such bifurcation in Cenvat Credit Rules.

The parent company may register and pay service tax under ‘Business Support Service’. Even otherwise, such debit may attract service tax under ‘Business Support Services’.

Input Service Distributor

7. A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service. Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office will be registered with Central Excise as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and it will have to issue invoice to the manufacturer or producer or service provider. They have to apply for registration in form ST-1.

7.1 Who is ‘input service distributor’ - As per rule 2(m), "input service distributor" means an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be.

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); ‘invoice, bill or challan’ issued by an ‘input service distributor’ under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

7.2 Distribution of credit - The ‘Input Service Distributor’ shall distribute Cenvat Credit in respect of service tax, among its manufacturing units providing output service. Whether garden maintenance service (With using materials/without using materials) is taxable? If yes, under which services it is taxable?

It should come under ‘Management, Maintenance or repair’ service , since that head covers both movable as well as immovable property. It does not make any difference whether it is with materials or without materials. You can claim deduction in respect of materials like plants, etc., but not in respect of consumables.

CENTRALISED OPERATIONS We are a Gas Distribution Company based at Gujarat. We are having CNG Station at various locations. We obtain excise Separate Registration of each CNG Station. Our queries are (1) Whether we are able to take CENVAT Credit on Excise Payable for Capital Goods? If yes, then whether only CENVAT credit on particular Capital goods used for a particular station only can be claimed? (2) Shall we claim excise on common pipe line which is partly used for CNG and partly for domestic gas, inspite of fact that domestic gas is not excisable goods? (3) Whether regarding the supplier invoice, the address of CNG Station has to be mentioned or not on that invoice or invoice made to Head Office address is sufficient to take Cenvat Credit?

(1) Since you have separate registration for each location, it is advisable to take separate credit only for each unit in respect of capital goods installed there. (2) Check tariff heading of pipeline. Mostly, it is 72 or 73 and, hence, does not fall within the definition of ‘capital goods’, as defined in the Cenvat Credit Rules. However, if some equipment does fall within the definition, you can take credit even if it is only partly used for taxable service. (3) It is highly advisable to mention address of CNG station in supplier’s invoice to avoid disputes and harassment from department. If this is not possible, invoice should be endorsed by HO in favour of CNG station with clear remark that these goods are for the particular unit and they have not taken any Cenvat credit at HO.

One of my clients has centralised registration. He has placed capital goods at various sites of the clients. Can the unit shift the capital goods to other sites of the clients after work at one site is completed ?

In respect of capital goods on which there was no credit taken, obviously no question arises. In other cases, if each unit is registered separately, then the first unit should pay ‘amount’ as per Cenvat credit rules and then other unit can take credit. However, in this case, since there is centralised registration, there is no problem, since there is no question of one unit paying duty and other unit taking credit. At the most, you may write letter informing department suitably (Don’t ask for permission. That will create a mess).

A unit having centralised registration is procuring inputs and input services at the sites where the work of the clients is going on. In view of the fact that the unit has taken centralized registration, will it be able to get credit of inputs and input services in the centralized office, if the billing of the supplier is addressed to this centralized office and inputs/input services are directly received at the work site? Or will the unit be required to avail service tax registration as a distributor for all these sites separately and then transfer the credit to centralized office? Here we would like to clarify that service tax registration certificate at present mentions the addresses of various sites at which work is going on.

Really, input service distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Further, Cenvat Credit Rules do not require one to one relationship. If there is centralised accounting and all records are available in HO, credit can be taken at HO. Of course, harassment from department cannot be ruled out. Hence, it is better to write a letter to the department about informing the procedure you are following.

We have branches at various places. Each branch is separately registered for purpose of service tax. In some cases, capital goods installed in one branch have to be shifted to other branch for various purposes like shortages, urgency, etc. We have received a demand that in such cases, Cenvat credit has to be reversed. Please advise.

It is true that technically, you should pay ‘amount’ while removing capital goods from one branch under ‘invoice’ and then take credit in other branch. However, practically, at operational level, such deep knowledge of service tax laws is difficult. You can argue that paying ‘amount’ in one branch and taking credit in other branch will be a revenue neutral exercise. There are many Tribunal decisions that substantive benefit cannot be lost for procedural lapses, particularly when the whole exercise is revenue neutral.

Firstly, definition of ‘input service’ is very wide. Any service in relation to your business is your ‘input service’. Any relation to manufacturing or provision of service is not envisaged in the inclusive part of the definition. Secondly, Cenvat Credit rules do not require one-to-one correlation. If you refer to Cenvat Credit Rules, all duties and taxes mentioned in rule 3(1) form a pool termed as ‘Cenvat Credit’. The rule 3(7) does not envisage bifurcation of ‘input service’ as you are envisaging from accountant’s perspective.

The pool of credit is common. It can be used for payment of excise duty or service tax or any other eligible tax or duty as specified in rule 3(4).

11. We agree that the issue is litigation prone. However, our views are as follows —

uInput Service Distributor is a facility. A facility cannot be a compulsion. It is required only when you want to ‘distribute’ Cenvat credit to more than one factories/service centre.

uDefinition of ‘input service’ is very wide. Any service in relation to business is your ‘input service’ for purpose of Cenvat credit.

uProvisions relating to distribution of Cenvat credit of input service by Head Office do not require that the distribution should be in a particular ratio or on a particular basis. Even if you register your HO as ‘Input Service Distributor, it is legally permissible to ‘distribute’ (allocate) entire credit to your HO factory itself, as is being done by you now.

uThus, getting registration as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and then ‘distributing’ entire credit to your HO factory itself will be an exercise in futility.

uThus, what you are doing today is perfectly legal and, in any case, ‘revenue neutral’.

In short, what you are doing is OK. However, to avoid unnecessary disputes, it is advisable to register HO as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and then ‘distribute the credit’. You should concentrate on work of value addition, instead of fritting away your energy on fruitless controversies.

. The assessee availed Cenvat credit on the quantity of LSHS. The Commissioner disallowed the credit holding that since fertilizers were exempted goods, credit on LSHS, even though used as fuel within the factory, was not allowable. On appeal, the Larger Bench of the Tribunal following the decision in CCE&C v. Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. 2006 (193) ELT 136 (Guj.) allowed the credit. The Supreme Court held that rule 6(1) is plenary. It restates a principle, namely, that Cenvat credit for duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products is not allowable. This principle is inbuilt in the very structure of the Cenvat Scheme. Sub-rule (1), therefore, merely highlights that principle. Sub-rule (1) covers all inputs, including fuel, whereas sub-rule (2) refers to non-fuel inputs. Sub-rule (2) covers a situation where common Cenvated inputs are used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product and exempted final product but the fuel input is excluded from that sub-rule. However, exclusion of fuel-input vis-a-vis non-fuel input would still fall in sub-rule (1). As stated above, sub-rule (1) is plenary and, hence, it cannot be said that because sub-rule (2) is inapplicable to fuel-input(s), Cenvat credit is automatically available to such inputs even if they are used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The cumulative reading of sub-rules (1) and (2) makes it abundantly clear that the circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), which, inter alia, require separate accounting of input, are not applicable to the fuel-input(s). However, the said sub-rule (2) nowhere says that the legal effect of sub-rule (1) will stand terminated in respect of fuel-inputs which do not fall in sub-rule (2). In other words, the legal effect of sub-rule (1) has to be applied to all inputs including fuel-inputs, only exception being non-fuel-inputs, for which one has to maintain separate accounts or in its absence, pay 8 per cent/10 per cent of the total price of the exempted final products. Therefore, sub-rule (1) of rule 6 shall apply in respect of goods used as ‘fuel’ and on such application, the credit will not be permissible on such quantity of fuel which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The above aspect had not been properly appreciated by the Gujarat High Court in the case of Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. (supra).

As per Supreme Court, it may be noted that litigation on interpretation of Cenvat Credit Rules has arisen on account of various conflicting decisions given by various Benches of CESTAT, the reason being that the rules have not been properly drafted. In the circumstances, no penalty was leviable, however, in order to decide the amount of duty payable by each of the assessees, the matter was to be remitted to the adjudicating authority to decide the amount of duty payable without penalty on reversal of credit to the extent of the input being used in the manufacture of exempted final products.

We have two units – one unit is paying duty and other unit is in Himachal Pradesh, which is exempt from duty. Is it required that Cenvat credit of services received at HO should be taken on proportionate basis? Please advise.

There is no provision to take credit on ‘proportionate basis’. You cannot apply costing principles for Cenvat credit when rule 7 or any other rule of Cenvat Credit Rules makes no such provision. Further, rule 7(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules provides that if some expenses are exclusively related to exempted product, then no credit is available. Thus, so long as expenses are not exclusively related to exempted final product, Cenvat credit is available. Hence, in my view, entire credit of service tax can be availed at HO, except that which is exclusively related to the unit manufacturing exempted goods.

Input Service Distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules uses the words ‘may distribute the Cenvat credit’. Thus, law does not say that credit can be availed only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. Moreover, you can distribute credit in any ratio. Thus, technically, even if you register your HO as input service distributor, you can take entire credit at Pune factory, itself. Cenvat Rules do not require one to one relationship.

To avoid litigation and petty disputes, it may be advisable to register HO as Input Service Distributor, though not legally required.

63. Clarity on supply by EV charging stations

The applicability of GST on supplies made by EV charging stations has sparked disputes, raising questions about classification, tax rates, and treatment under existing regulations.

A key area of ambiguity is whether the supply by EV charging stations should be classified as a supply of goods or services under GST regulations. This distinction significantly impacts the tax treatment of such transactions. Further complexities arise as to whether the supply should be considered the provision of electricity, which is exempt from GST, or a taxable supply categorised under HSN 8504 (Charger or charging station for electrically operated vehicles), attracting a GST rate of 5%. This lack of clarity has led to inconsistencies in tax compliance and interpretation.

Another notable disparity in this scenario is that consumers charging EVs at personal residences are not subject to GST, while those using commercial EV charging stations incur GST. This creates a serious inconsistency in the tax treatment of what is essentially the same transaction. Also, this gap results in a dual tax structure for the same end use, placing an undue financial burden on consumers utilising commercial facilities.

Additionally, the European Court of Justice, in the case of Digital Charging Solutions11, has addressed a similar issue & ruled that electricity supplied for charging electric vehicles is to be classified as a supply of ('electricity') goods, since electricity is considered tangible property. This perspective could serve as a reference point for aligning GST policies in India.

It is therefore recommended that the supply by EV charging stations be explicitly clarified as the supply of electricity (in line with the global tax treatment), exempt from GST. This will promote and accelerate the growth of the electric vehicle industry and infrastructure in India.

64. Inclusion of inter-state RCM transactions for the purposes of the Input Service Distributor ('ISD') mechanism

Under GST, a supplier of goods and services may receive a single invoice at common office(s) for the procurement of services that are used by its other units. Since these services are common to multiple units, the common office(s) cannot claim ITC of the entire GST amount. To address this, the common office is required to register as an ISD under GST and distribute the ITC to the relevant units by issuing invoices in compliance with the GST legislation.

Notably, with effect from 01-04-202512, the ISD registration is made mandatory for common offices receiving common ITC for deemed distinct persons. The Finance Act, 2024, has substituted the definitions of ISD under Sections 2(6) and 20 of the CGST Act to include the distribution of common ITC in respect of invoices for intra-state RCM services.

To further extend the benefit of availment of common ITC on inter-state RCM transactions under the ISD mechanism, based on the recommendation of the 55th GST Council meeting, it is expected to amend Section 2(61) and Section 20(1) of the CGST Act by including a reference to supplies subject to tax under Section 5(3) and 5(4) of the IGST Act in the said provisions. And, it is further expected that Section 20(2) of the CGST Act and Rule 39(1A) of the CGST Rules be suitably amended to be made effective from 01-04-2025.

Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017 provides for the refund of the balance of ITC where export is made without payment of tax under a bond or a letter of undertaking. Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017 provides the refund formula for the same as under:

Refund amount = [(Turnover of zero-rated supply of goods + Turnover of zero-rated supply of services)/Adjusted total turnover] * Net ITC

In the given formula, regarding the turnover of the zero-rated supply of goods, the Explanation to Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules13 provides that the value of goods exported out of India would be taken as the lower of the following values:

(a)

Free on Board (FOB) value declared in the Shipping Bill or Bill of Export form, as the case may be; or

(b)

The value is declared in the tax invoice or bill of supply.

Notably, for the export of goods under CIF contracts, the exporter must separately report the FOB value of the goods, as well as insurance and freight expenses, on the shipping bill. The FOB value reported in the shipping bill would always be less than the value as per the tax invoice. In this case, the GSTN system uses the FOB value as per the shipping bill. Thus, the refund amount would always be reduced proportionately to the value of insurance and freight expenses.

This would result in a loss of the refund amount for the insurance and freight costs. This loss would be significant in cases where the cost of packing and transporting comprises a considerable proportion of the value. The formula for calculating ITC refunds should be rationalised, and, for CIF contracts, the CIF value of the goods should be used in the calculation.

CENVAT CREDIT

Role and obligations of input service distributor

‘Input service distributor’ is a new concept introduced by CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, with effect from 10-9-2004. It is commonly observed that public limited companies have their registered/head office in a State and a number of industrial units manufacturing excisable goods or branches rendering services at locations in various places. Since no manufacturing activity or rendering of services takes place at the head office, the amount of service tax so paid cannot be used as CENVAT Credit at the head office, and the amount turns into an irrecoverable loss. To mitigate the hardship, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, allow such offices to distribute the credit earned as ‘input service distributor’ against invoice to be issued just like a service provider. The role and obligations of such offices as ‘input services distributor’ have been laid down in the Service Tax Rules, 1994, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005. With reference to these Rules, in this article, the author explains the role and obligations of an ‘input service distributor’.

AJAY KUMAR GARG*

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is a new concept introduced by CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, with effect from September 10, 2004. This concept has been devised to provide a special dispensation in respect of services received at an office/branch which itself is not engaged in any manufacturing activity or rendering of any service.

It is commonly observed that public limited companies have their registered/head office in a State and a number of industrial units manufacturing excisable goods or branches rendering services at locations in various places. The head office receives several services such as telephone, sale promotion, business auxiliary, custom house agent’s services, rail/air reservation services, etc., for which it pays service tax to service providers. However, since no manufacturing activity or rendering of services takes place at the head office, the amount of service tax so paid cannot be used as CENVAT Credit at the head office, and the amount turns into an irrecoverable loss.

To mitigate this hardship, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, allow such offices to distribute the credit earned as ‘input service distributor’ against invoice to be issued just like a service provider. The role and obligations of such offices as ‘input services distributor’ have been laid down in the Service Tax Rules, 1994, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005.

Input service distributor

2. An ‘input service distributor’ has been defined under rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, to mean ‘an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be.’

Registration

3. In terms of section 69(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, read with Notification No. 26/2005-ST, dated June 7, 2005, with effect from June 16, 2005, an input service distributor is required to obtain registration under service tax law.

Rule 3(1) of Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 requires an input service distributor to apply for registration in revised Form ST-1 (vide Notification No. 32/2005-ST, dated October 20, 2005), within 30 days from June 16, 2005 or date of commencement of business, whichever is later. Other procedure relating to registration, applicable to service providers in general, shall apply to input service distributors as well.

No liability to pay service tax

4. The role of an ‘input service distributor’ is only to receive and distribute CENVAT Credit in respect of taxable services received by it. It is not liable to pay any service tax since it is not engaged in actual rendering of taxable services.

Attention of the Board has been invited to the difficulties faced by the manufacturers in availing the credit under rule 57G/57T where :

(i)

the Bill of Entry has been filed in the name of the registered office/head office of the manufacturer for the inputs to be used in his factory.

(ii)

imported goods lying in customs dock area/bonded warehouse are diverted to manufacturing units in whose name Bill of Entry has not been filed.

(iii)

domestic duty paid goods consigned to a manufacturing unit are diverted in whole or part from a duty paid godown of the manufacturer or such diversion is affected in transit.

2. The issue has been examined by the Board.

3. It has been decided that credit should not be denied where the Bill of Entry is in the name of the registered office/head office provided that :—

(a)

the entire consignment covered by the said Bill of Entry is received in the factory in original packed conditions.

(b)

triplicate copy of Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system is endorsed by the registered office/head office to the effect that consignment covered by the Bill of Entry are delivered to the manufacturing unit for availing credit.

4. Where the imported goods are still in Customs dock area and the manufacturer- importer decides to divert/transfer the goods, a declaration by the manufacturer- importer can be made on the reverse of triplicate copy of Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system by the manufacturer-importer that consignments are being delivered to the unit (name of the unit) for availing credit and endorsed by the proper Officer of Customs for enabling the manufacturing unit to avail credit.

5. In cases where the imported goods are lying in the bonded warehouse from where diversion takes place either of entire consignment or part consignment, credit can be permitted provided ex-bond Bill of Entry is filed for such entire/part consignments and that a declaration is made on the reverse of the said ex-bond triplicate copy of the Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system to the effect that consignments are delivered to a unit (name of the unit) for availing credit.

6. In all cases duty-paying documents on the basis of which credit has been availed in aforesaid cases, should be submitted to the Range Superintendent for the necessary verification and defacing/endorsement.

7. In case of split consignments and other types of cases not covered by the preceding paragraphs the inputs can be cleared on the payment of duty as envisaged under rule 57F/57S and on the basis of such duty-paying documents credit can be availed.

41.3-4 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

41.3-5 GAR-7 challan when service tax paid by person other than service provider

In some cases, service tax is payable by service receiver instead of service provider.

In such case, the recipient of service/insurance company will pay service tax by way of GAR-7 challan. Such challan is eligible for availing Cenvat credit [rule 9(1)(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules] - same view in CCE v. Ambika Overseas (2012) 278 ELT 524 (CESTAT SMB).

Storage of inputs outside the factory

21.2-2 Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant / Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

The view seems correct for the following reasons.

The words used in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are 'invoice, challan or Bill'. Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules specified the document as 'Invoice'. This indicates that in case of service tax, specific nomenclature is not essential.

In fact, first and second proviso to rule 4A(1) uses the term 'any document, by whatever name called'. Thus, rules do envisage flexibility in nomenclature depending on trade and business practices. Different practices are followed in different trades. Nomenclature can vary from trade to trade or business to business.

As per rule 5(1) of Service Tax Rules, the records maintained by assessee including computerised data maintained by assessee in accordance with various other laws are acceptable. Thus, private documents maintained in normal course of business are acceptable. No special records or registers or change in business practices is envisaged. This also indicates that law does not envisage that trade should change its normal business practices.

As per Explanation (c) to section 67 of Finance Act, 1994, "Gross amount charged" includes payment by cheque, credit card, deduction from account and any form of payment by issue of credit notes or debit notes and book adjustment. Thus, charging of any amount by debit note and credit note has been accepted.

26.3 Invoice raised by manufacturer of inputs will contain details of excise duty paid on total quantity. The wholesaler or distributor may supply the goods received from manufacturer to more than one buyer, dealers or sub-dealers.

Cenvatable Invoice - In a normal commercial Invoice raised by wholesaler, distributor or dealer, excise duty will not be charged separately. In fact the dealer cannot charge excise duty in his invoice separately as he has not paid the same.

Rule 11(7) of Central Excise Rules states that provisions of rule 11 (which is applicable to manufacturers) shall apply mutatis mutandis to goods supplied by a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer. In addition, as per rule 9(4) of Cenvat Credit Rules, Amount of duty actually paid on goods should be indicated in the invoice of dealer on pro rata basis. [It should not be 'charged', but merely 'indicated'].

As per rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, Invoice shall contain -

(a)

Registration Number

(b)

Name of consignee

(c)

Description and classification of goods

(d)

Time and date of removal

(e)

Mode of transport and vehicle registration number

(f)

Rate of duty

(g)

Quantity and Value of goods

(h)

Duty payable on the goods.

(i)

Address of jurisdictional Central Excise Division (added w.e.f. 1-4-2007).

(j)

In case of a proprietary concern or a business owned by Hindu undivided family, the name of the proprietor or Hindu undivided family, as the case may be, shall also be mentioned in the invoice (inserted w.e.f. 25-1-2008).

Thus, details of manufacturer or first stage dealer (from whom goods were purchased) are legally not required to be indicated in the Invoice. However, these were required under earlier provisions, and dealers are blindly using the earlier forms though legally those details are now not required.

Cenvat credit cannot be denied merely because details of Cenvat credit were given in annexure to the Invoice - Nestle India v. CCE (2013) 287 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB).

Excise duty should not be charged separately to buyer in invoice - A dealer is required to indicate in his invoice the excise duty paid on goods by the buyer. However, this should not be separately charged to buyer. Details of excise duty paid by the manufacturer should only be shown separately in the invoice. The amount of excise should not be recovered from buyer separately showing it as 'excise duty'.

Dealer should not issue another invoice - 'Dealer's Invoice for Cenvat' means the normal commercial invoice raised by dealer, only containing additional particulars of the excise duty paid and other details as required. Dealer should not issue commercial invoice plus additional invoice for excise Cenvat purposes. [Mumbai-III Trade Notice No. 63, Vadodara No. 119/94 dated 2-9-94; Nagpur No. 90/56/94 dated 19-9-94].

In CCE v. Graphite (I) (2007) 212 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB), Cenvat credit on basis of 'cash memo' was held as admissible. It was observed that hyper technicalities should not be made to disallow Cenvat credit.

In CCE v. Gwalior Chemicals (2011) 274 ELT 97 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of document titles 'Debit Note cum Bill'.

The view seems correct for the following reasons.

Section 67 of Finance Act, states that 'gross amount charged' includes debit notes. Thus, charging service tax by debit note is recognised by Statute itself. A rule cannot override provisions of Statute.

The words used in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are 'invoice, challan or Bill'. Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules specified the document as 'Invoice'. This indicates that in case of service tax, specific nomenclature is not essential.

In fact, first and second proviso to rule 4A(1) uses the term 'any document, by whatever name called'. Thus, rules do envisage flexibility in nomenclature depending on trade and business practices. Different practices are followed in different trades. Nomenclature can vary from trade to trade or business to business.

As per rule 5(1) of Service Tax Rules, the records maintained by assessee including computerised data maintained by assessee in accordance with various other laws are acceptable. Thus, private documents maintained in normal course of business are acceptable. No special records or registers or change in business practices is envisaged. This also indicates that law does not envisage that trade should change its normal business practices.

As per Explanation (c) to section 67 of Finance Act, 1994, "Gross amount charged" includes payment by cheque, credit card, deduction from account and any form of payment by issue of credit notes or debit notes and book adjustment. Thus, charging of any amount by debit note and credit note has been accepted.
